claims.text: The name humppa was invented by Antero Alpola for a radio show in the 1950s.
Humppa is related to jazz and fast foxtrot, played two beats to a bar.
The band probably used a tuba, as the sound of tuba on the first beat is like hump, the second beat coming as a pa.
One form of Humppa dance is related to one-step, which arrived in Finland 1913.
The second Humppa form is related to two-step, which came to Finland in 1910.
A third form of dance, Nilkku, is based on a slow, slow, quick, quick rhythm.
The revival meant that humppa had become the most popular music and dancing form for older people and for the countryside's youth in the Eastern and South-Eastern parts of the country.

sections.origins_and_history: The fatele originated as a traditional dance-song in Tuvalu. It faced suppression in the 1860s due to missionary influence but evolved in the 20th century, incorporating elements of the Samoan siva dance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Traditionally performed sitting or kneeling by women. Modern performances feature women standing in lines, enacting stories through arm and body movements while men provide rhythmic accompaniment.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features singing led by older men in a meeting hall (maneapa). Percussion is provided by beating hands on mats, empty cabin cracker cans, or wooden tea chests.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear titi fakamanumanu (coconut leaf skirts), titi kaulama (layered skirts), teuga saka (tops), and various floral garlands and bands. Performances occur in community spaces like the maneapa.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at weddings, church festivals, and to honor prominent visitors. It is a competitive tradition that serves as a community celebration.
sections.notable_figures: Gerd Koch (anthropologist who recorded traditional songs in 1960-1961).
sections.regional_variants: Shared tradition between Tuvalu and Tokelau.
sections.lineage: Influenced by Samoan siva dance and European melody and harmony.

sections.origins_and_history: Western swing arose in the late 1920s and early 1930s out of house parties, ranch dances, and small-town dance halls across Texas and Oklahoma. Pioneers like Bob Wills, Milton Brown, and the Light Crust Doughboys blended traditional fiddle tunes with jazz and blues. By the late 1930s and 1940s, the style achieved massive popularity, broadcasting via powerful radio stations like KVOO and packing ballrooms across the Southwest and California.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers engaged in simple couples dances, including two-steps and the Lindy Hop, enhanced with Western twirls. By 1937, the jitterbug gained immense popularity in the West, characterized by a style that was smoother and more subdued than the all-out boogie woogie.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed by a hot string band featuring fiddles, mandolin, upright bass, electric and acoustic guitars, and banjos, frequently augmented by drums, saxophones, trumpets, trombones, pianos, accordion, and the distinctive electrically amplified steel guitar.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers gathered in expansive ballrooms, dance pavilions, and nightspots such as Cain's Ballroom in Tulsa, the Crystal Springs Dance Pavilion in Fort Worth, and the Venice Pier Ballroom in California, often drawing thousands of attendees on Saturday nights.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Saturday night dances served as the core of social life for working-class communities throughout Texas, Oklahoma, and California, providing a vital recreational outlet amid the hardships of the Great Depression and World War II.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Bob Wills, co-founder of the Light Crust Doughboys and leader of the Texas Playboys; Milton Brown, pioneer of Western swing vocal styling; Spade Cooley, bandleader dubbed the 'King of Western Swing'; and Johnnie Lee Wills and Hank Thompson, who carried the tradition forward.
sections.regional_variants: The genre developed distinct regional hubs, originating in the Texas-Oklahoma borderlands and expanding dramatically during World War II into a thriving California scene centered around Los Angeles area ballrooms.
sections.lineage: Western swing developed as an outgrowth of country music and jazz. It subsequently influenced later genres including honky-tonk, rockabilly, and country rock.

sections.origins_and_history: Pungmul is rooted in the dure collective labor farming culture, rural holidays, community-building events, and shamanistic rituals. During the Japanese colonial era (1910–1945), colonial authorities promoted the term nongak to limit its scope and suppress its cultural meaning. In the late 1960s and 1970s, it gained new life in political protests during the pro-democracy movement. In 1978, performers created SamulNori, a seated indoor staging that popularized the tradition globally.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Most performances take place outdoors with dozens of players in constant motion, featuring group formations (jinpuri), solo performances by the lead gong player (Sangsoe Noleum), hat-streamer twirling (Sangmonori), hourglass drum solos (Suljanggu Noleum), small drum dances (Sogo Noleum), and satirical character skits (japsaek).
sections.music_and_instruments: Drumming is the central element of pungmul, utilizing five major instruments: the kkwaenggwari (small handheld gong), janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), jing (gong), and sogo (small handle drum). Wind instruments such as the taepyeongso (hojeok, senap, or nalari) also accompany the drummers. Rhythm patterns are known as jangdan.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear colorful costumes, most commonly featuring a flowery version of the Buddhist gokkal head-dress. Advanced troupe members wear sangmo hats with long ribbons spun via knee bends. Settings are traditionally outdoor village streets, fields, and community spaces.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically played during farm work, lunar holidays, village community events, shamanistic rituals, and fundraising. In the late 20th century, it became an important artistic medium for political protest and expression during the pro-democracy movement.
sections.notable_figures: Kim Duk-soo, Kim Yong-bae, Sim U-seong, Kim Swoo Geun, Kim Bong Jun, and Yi Jong-hun.
sections.regional_variants: Recognized in five primary regional styles under South Korean cultural property designation: Jinju Samcheonpo nongak (yeongnam style), Pyeongtaek nongak (utdari style), Iri nongak (honam udo style), Gangneung nongak (yeongdong style), and Imsil Pilbong nongak (honam jwado style, known for rapid rhythms and varying formations).
sections.lineage: Rooted in ancient agricultural and shamanistic traditions; gave rise to modern staged percussion genres like SamulNori and shares historical ties with itinerant Namsadang troupes.

claims.text: Pungmul is a Korean folk music tradition that includes drumming, dancing, and singing.
Pungmul is rooted in the dure (collective labor) farming culture.
Each group is led by a kkwaenggwari small handheld gong player.
Older scholars often describe this tradition as nongak, a term meaning farmers' music whose usage arose during the colonial era.
In an advanced troupe all performers may wear sangmo, which are hats with long ribbon attached to them that players can spin and flip in intricate patterns powered by knee bends.

sections.origins_and_history: The oral tradition places the origins of the morna on Boa Vista Island in the 18th century, potentially evolving from a cross between local working choros and the introduced lundum. By the 19th century, it was a fully formed genre, with compositions like 'Brada Maria' documented around 1870. The 2nd period, led by Eugénio Tavares in the early 20th century on Brava Island, introduced slower tempos and romantic lyricism focused on love and separation. The 3rd period in the 1930s and 1940s saw São Vicente composer B. Leza incorporate Brazilian-influenced passing chords, expanding harmonic possibilities beyond the traditional cycle of fifths. The 4th period (1950s-1970s) coincided with the rise of the coladeira and the incorporation of political and homeland themes. Recent years have seen increased artistic freedom, with contemporary composers experimenting with chord sequences and fusions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: As a dance the morna is a ballroom dance, danced in pairs. The performers dance with an arm embracing the partner, while with the other arm they hold hands. The dancing is made through two body swings to one side in a music's bar, while in the next bar the swinging is to the other side.
sections.music_and_instruments: Characterized by a lento tempo and a 2-beat bar (sometimes 4), traditional morna relies on a harmonic structure based on a cycle of fifths and is almost always monotonic. The melody features frequent syncopation, extending notes from the end of a bar to the strong beat of the next. The primary instrument is the guitar (*violão*), utilizing a specific fingerpicking and strumming technique called *mãozada* that articulates a thumb-driven bass line with arpeggiated or rhythmic chords. Ensembles also incorporate cavaquinhos, ten or twelve-string violas, violins (*rabecas*), pianos, and various percussion instruments.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at key life events such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. Central themes include universal subjects like love, as well as distinctively Cape Verdean realities: departure abroad, return, saudade, love for the homeland, and the sea.
sections.notable_figures: Cesária Évora, Eugénio Tavares, B. Leza (Francisco Xavier da Cruz), Bana, Celina Pereira, Teté Alhinho, Jorge Monteiro, Manuel de Novas, Ildo Lobo.
sections.regional_variants: Boa Vista morna is the oldest variant, characterized by a quicker tempo (andante ~96 bpm), rubato style, simpler structure, and satirical or social themes. Brava morna features a slower tempo (lento ~60 bpm), strong romanticism, rhymes, and a rigid meter. São Vicente morna shares the slower tempo of Brava but incorporates enriched passing chords, wider non-rigid themes, and lacks strict rhyming.
sections.lineage: Considered by some authors to be a cross between local choros and the lundum. It served as a precursor and contemporary to the coladeira.

sections.origins_and_history: The Semah is rooted in the Alevi-Bektaşi belief system, which is based on admiration for Ali. It is a living tradition transmitted orally through generations.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in circular patterns and rotate around their own axes. Men and women dance together. The right palm faces upward and the left palm faces downward.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is played on the 'saz' long-necked lute. The rhythm is typically the 'aksak' meter.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in 'cemevleri' (Alevi meetinghouses) or during festivals like the Hacı Bektaş Veli Festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is one of the twelve services of the 'Cem' ritual. It symbolizes the unity of man with God and nature.
sections.notable_figures: Hacı Bektaş Veli is a central figure in the tradition.
sections.regional_variants: Forms include 'kirklar semahı' (sema of the forty) and 'turnalar semahı' (crane sema).
sections.lineage: Part of the broader Sufi tradition of 'Sama' (listening/remembrance), but distinct in its Alevi-Bektaşi practice.

claims.text: Semah is a set of mystical and aesthetic body movements in rhythmic harmony, constituting one of the twelve main services in Cem rituals.
The Semah is performed by both men and women side by side.
The music is determined by the aksak rhythm.
The right hand faces up and the left hand faces down.
The Semah was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2010.

sections.origins_and_history: Moshing originated in the southern California hardcore punk scene, particularly Huntington Beach and Long Beach around 1978, evolving from the 1970s English pogo. Through the 1980s, it spread to Washington, D.C., Boston, and New York, where cross-pollination with heavy metal gave rise to the term 'mosh' via bands like Stormtroopers of Death and Anthrax. In the 1990s, grunge and festivals like Lollapalooza brought the mosh pit into mainstream consciousness, followed by later adoption in hip-hop and electronic dance music.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Participants push, slam, or run into each other inside a mosh pit. Variations include the Huntington Beach Strut (strutting in a circle while swinging arms), the Wall of Death (two halves of the audience charging at each other), circle pits (running counter-clockwise in a circle), and hardcore dancing (two-stepping, floorpunching, and windmilling).
sections.music_and_instruments: Performed to aggressive styles of live music featuring electric guitars, bass guitars, drums, and aggressive vocals, spanning punk rock, heavy metal, grunge, hardcore, hip-hop, and electronic dance music.
sections.costume_and_setting: Typically performed in concert venues, festivals, and underground music clubs. Participants generally wear casual street clothing, and sources note it is indispensable to avoid wearing glasses due to the high risk of eye injury.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Occurs during live music performances as a form of passionate fan feedback, release of energy, and underground cultural expression, though it has also been viewed by some as a manifestation of aggressive bullying.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Mike Marine (credited with the Huntington Beach Strut), H.R. of Bad Brains, Scott Ian and Billy Milano of Stormtroopers of Death, and artists associated with its mainstream spread like Billy Corgan and Travis Scott.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the Huntington Beach Strut in Southern California, Boston thrash and pig piles in Boston, New York hardcore style, psychobilly wrecking, and hip-hop pits which tend to feature jumping in unison rather than violent slamming.
sections.lineage: Directly descended from the 1970s English punk pogo, subsequently branching into regional hardcore styles, heavy metal moshing, grunge pits, and modern hip-hop raging.

sections.origins_and_history: The twist traces its stylistic lineage to African-American and African traditions, with historians Marshall and Jean Stearns noting that a pelvic dance motion called the twist came to America from the Congo during slavery. Early iterations appeared in blackface minstrelsy with Joel Walker Sweeney's 'Vine Twist' and the early 20th-century craze 'Mess Around'. Blues artists referenced the concept decades prior to the 1950s boom, including Bo Carter's 'Twist It Babe' in 1931 and Jelly Roll Morton's 'Winin' Boy Blues'. The modern dance took definitive shape among teenagers in the late 1950s, catalyzed by Hank Ballard's original song and catapulted to global fame by Chubby Checker's 1960 television debut.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The twist is performed standing with feet approximately shoulder-width apart. The hips, torso, and legs rotate on the balls of the feet as a single unit, with feet grinding back and forth on the floor as if putting out a cigarette. Knees are bent slightly, and arms are held out from the body, bent at the elbow. Hips swivel from side to side while upper body sways, with dancers maintaining a low posture and very little vertical motion, requiring no physical contact between partners.
sections.music_and_instruments: Driven by upbeat rock and roll instrumentation featuring electric guitars, drums, piano, and saxophone, alongside energetic vocal performances. Hit recordings featured driving backbeats and call-and-response structures designed to propel continuous physical movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Danced in informal youth settings, discotheques, and television stages. Costumes reflected early 1960s casual wear, ranging from teenage skirts and trousers to sophisticated club attire at venues like New York's Peppermint Lounge.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Functioned as a spontaneous youth craze that bridged social divides, transforming rock music into a mass-market phenomenon while sparking generational debates over its suggestive pelvic motions.
sections.notable_figures: Chubby Checker, Hank Ballard, Dick Clark, Joey Dee, Bill Haley, Sam Cooke, Bo Diddley.
sections.regional_variants: Exported internationally, yielding localized versions such as Mexico's 'Spanish Twist' and 'Florida Twist' by Bill Haley, French yé-yé adaptations by Johnny Hallyday and Eddy Mitchell, and British pop versions.
sections.lineage: Influenced subsequent 1960s fad dances including the Jerk, the Pony, the Watusi, the Mashed Potato, the Monkey, and the Funky Chicken.

sections.origins_and_history: Developed from mid-19th-century prize walks on Southern US plantations, the cakewalk was exhibited at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia. It moved into minstrel shows and eventually Broadway, starring performers like Dora Dean and Charles E. Johnson, before becoming an international sensation in Paris in 1903.
sections.how_it_is_danced: A lively partnered vernacular jazz dance featuring processional walking, high-stepping kicks, struts, slides, and an erect upper body tilted backward, alternating with frantic jumps and turns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Notated in a 2/4 time signature with an oompah rhythm, incorporating syncopation, polyrhythms, and habanera rhythms. Historically played with banjos and violins, it heavily shaped the development of ragtime.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wore handed-down finery including top hats, swallow-tail coats, large bow ties, canes, and long ruffled hoop skirts. Settings ranged from plantation yards to rented halls with banked spectator tiers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during Sunday gatherings and nighttime parties as a recreational pastime and a covert satire of white aristocratic European dances, with slaveholders awarding cakes to winning couples.
sections.notable_figures: Dora Dean, Charles E. Johnson, Tom Fletcher, Eugénie Fougère, Aida Overton Walker, Will Marion Cook.
sections.regional_variants: Spread from Florida across Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and New York, reaching international popularity in Paris and influencing early tango styles in Buenos Aires.
sections.lineage: Rooted in African American plantation culture, influenced by the ring shout, and serving as a direct precursor and sibling style to ragtime music.

sections.origins_and_history: The pogo emerged around 1976 during the early days of London's punk scene. Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious claimed to have invented the dance to mock non-punk attendees, while others attribute it to his leather poncho restricting movement or his frantic jumping while playing saxophone. It served as an anti-disco movement to counter mainstream rhythm.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers jump up and down while either remaining on the spot or moving around. The classic version involves keeping the torso stiff, arms rigid at the sides, and legs close together like a pogo stick. Variations allow for thrashing torsos, flailing arms, kicking legs, spinning in the air, and horizontal pushing.
sections.music_and_instruments: Associated primarily with punk rock, heavy metal, hardcore, and alternative rock genres. Instruments typically include electric guitars, bass guitars, drums, and occasional saxophones. The musical style is fast-paced and aggressive, designed to counter regular disco beats.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in underground music venues, clubs, and massive outdoor festivals (such as Monsters of Rock or large punk/metal gatherings). Attire reflects punk, underground, and counter-culture styles, historically including leather jackets, ponchos, and everyday street clothing.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during live music performances of aggressive genres like punk and heavy metal. It serves as an expression of underground counter-culture, anti-establishment sentiment, and raw energy, underpinned by an unwritten code of community solidarity and safety for fallen dancers.
sections.notable_figures: Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols is widely credited with inventing or popularizing the dance. Other early figures associated with its lore include Shane MacGowan, Viv Albertine, and Glen Matlock. In Argentina, rock singer Indio Solari is renowned for fronting massive crowds during famous pogo events.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include slam dancing (slamming into others), moshing (pushing in a crowd without high vertical jumps), stage diving, slamming from the stage, wall of death (two halves of a crowd crashing together), and circle pits (running in a circle). Local names include mosh, tangana, olla, pateo, foso, mocha, and agite.
sections.lineage: The pogo is a direct precursor to modern moshing and slam dancing, sharing historical proximity with ska skanking and rockabilly traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: The origins of Seungmu are uncertain, with little extant evidence. Some theories link it to the monk Wonhyo or to the mocking of upper-class priests. Once prohibited during the Joseon dynasty, it was transformed into a folk dance by kisaengs and later refashioned into stage art by Han Sŏngjun in 1936.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed solo. It begins with the dancer crouched on the ground, slowly expanding their motion. The dancer uses long, white sleeves to create expressive shapes in the air. The performance involves eight rhythmic cycles that dictate changes in mood and footwork, moving from slow, heavy rhythms to faster, more complex drum-driven sequences.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by eight rhythmic cycles: yeombul, dodeuri, taryeong, jajin taryeong, gutgeori, dwit gutgeori, gujeong nori, and saesanjo. The 'bubgo' (drum) is the most important instrument, serving as a central element of the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dancer wears a 'jangsam' (a robe with long, white sleeves) and a 'gokkal' (a white hood). The costume is described as radiant with elegant lines.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Seungmu is a form of art that communicates to the public. It symbolizes the birth of the universe, the four azimuths, the course of life, and human emotions like joy, wrath, and sorrow.
sections.notable_figures: Lee Mae Bang (deceased 2015), Kim Myo Seon, Kim Myung Ja, and Han Young-suk are noted as masters or master assistants of this tradition.
sections.regional_variants: The dance was improvised in variegated forms in different regions until the 1930s when various styles were archived and choreographed.
sections.lineage: The dance is a descendant of folk art traditions and shares commonalities with Buddhist ritual dances, though it is distinct from them.

sections.origins_and_history: Investigations trace the siciliana back to 14th-century poetic-musical compositions inspired by Sicilian folk songs. It evolved through the Renaissance strambotto and 17th-century recitar cantando before codifying into Baroque instrumental and operatic forms. The earliest reference to the term regarding a dance appears in Tommaso Garzoni's 1599 work 'La piazza universale di tutte le professioni del mondo'.

sections.origins_and_history: The fouetté en tournant was introduced in the Grand Pas d'azione of the ballet Cinderella on December 17, 1893, with choreography by Lev Ivanov, Enrico Cecchetti, and Marius Petipa, and music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. Pierina Legnani performed 32 consecutive fouettés without traveling, a feat reported by St. Petersburg Gazette critic Konstantin Skalkovski. Legnani repeated this in Swan Lake (1895), and Mathilde Kschesinskaya later achieved the same milestone.
sections.how_it_is_danced: A fouetté turn begins standing on one flat foot in plié with the knee bent. The working leg is extended and whipped to the side to create momentum, then pulled into a retiré or passé position while the supporting foot rises to relevé or en pointe. This creates the angular momentum needed for a rotation in place.
sections.music_and_instruments: The historic introduction of 32 consecutive fouettés in Cinderella featured music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. The movement is subsequently incorporated into the grand pas and major ballets such as Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performing 32 consecutive fouettés is considered a bravura demonstration of a ballerina's strength, stamina, and technique. It is a highly difficult feat that many dancers can execute on only one side, usually the right.

sections.origins_and_history: The roots of the polska are traced to 17th-century Polish court influences interacting with indigenous Nordic musical structures and older triple-meter folk songs.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced primarily as a couple, featuring walking promenades, counter-clockwise upper-body turns (bakmes), and rapid clockwise rotations (pols) executed in triple time.

sections.regional_variants: Includes Norwegian pols and springar, Swedish slängpolskas in Småland, and diverse community styles across Dalarna and Uppland.

claims.text: The Slängpolska is a Swedish folk dance whose name comes from the Swedish word for toss, throw, or chuck.
Slängpolskor are divided into two major types, with the first type featuring stationary dancing for two or four people focusing on holds.
A typical Type 1 slängpolska step consists of four steps over three beats: one long, two short, one long.
The second type involves couples moving counterclockwise around the room periphery at a high tempo with a tossing feeling and rotational jumps.

sections.origins_and_history: The pas de deux originated in the mid-18th century as a ballet entrée featuring couples performing identical steps, evolving through the Baroque and Romantic periods to symbolize romantic love. By the 19th century, Marius Petipa established the grand pas de deux structure with entrée, adagio, two variations, and coda, elevating the male dancer's role and making it a ballet highlight.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The grand pas de deux begins with an entrée where dancers enter and acknowledge each other. The adagio features slow, supported movements with the male dancer lifting and steadying the ballerina. Then, each dancer performs a solo variation showcasing leaps and turns—the male first, then the female. The coda reunites them in a fast, virtuosic finale. Technique involves pointe work for the ballerina, supported balances, and precise timing. The male partner provides physical support and acts as a 'virtual barre' during balancing. Beginners start with basic partnering and slow adagio movements.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for pas de deux is composed in classical ballet style, supporting the five-part structure with tempo shifts from slow adagio to fast coda. Orchestral scores by composers like Tchaikovsky accompany famous pas de deux, emphasizing lyrical melodies and rhythmic clarity to match the dancers' movements.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes typically reflect classical ballet attire: the ballerina wears a tutu and pointe shoes, while the male dancer wears tights and fitted jackets. The setting is usually a proscenium stage within a full-length ballet production, with lighting and scenery enhancing the romantic or dramatic theme of the pas de deux.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The pas de deux is performed as a central highlight in classical ballets, symbolizing romantic partnership and emotional connection between the dancers. It often marks a climactic moment within a ballet's narrative, showcasing the principal dancers' technical and expressive abilities.
sections.notable_figures: Marius Petipa is the key historical figure who formalized the grand pas de deux structure in the 19th century. Famous dancers like Mikhail Baryshnikov and Gregory Hines have performed notable pas de deux, including in film adaptations.
sections.regional_variants: While the grand pas de deux structure is standard in classical ballet worldwide, contemporary choreographers have created duos for same-gender pairs and incorporated more acrobatic movements, expanding the form beyond its traditional romantic male-female pairing.
sections.lineage: The pas de deux descends from 18th-century ballet entrées and evolved through Romantic ballet into the grand pas de deux codified by Petipa. It remains a foundational element of classical ballet repertoire, influencing contemporary duet choreography.

claims.text: In ballet, a pas de deux is a dance duet in which two dancers perform ballet steps together.
A grand pas de deux typically has five parts: entrée, adagio, two variations, and a coda.
The adagio features graceful partnering with the male dancer supporting the ballerina in lifts and balances.
Marius Petipa introduced the grand pas de deux format in the late 19th century.
The male dancer's variation is usually performed first, followed by the ballerina's variation.
The coda is a fast-paced conclusion recapitulating earlier segments, ending in a grand musical climax.
The pas de deux symbolizes the love of a couple and illustrates poetic moments in ballet.
The male dancer often acts as a 'third leg' providing balance and support during pointe work.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition originated from British and European dances like the Virginia Reel and quadrilles, which were adapted by American settlers. Early 19th-century 'junkets' or 'heel-burners' were casual, all-night affairs. The influence of African musical traditions, such as 'patting juba' and the use of the banjo, was fundamental to the development of early American dance rhythms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances are categorized into couple, group, and line formations. Couple dancing relies on a lead-and-follow dynamic where the man sets the pace. The movement is characterized by a flat-footed glide. In line dancing, participants perform fixed, choreographed steps in rows. There is no single 'correct' way to perform many of these dances, as regional variations are common.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is primarily country-western, though it draws from pop and bluegrass. Historically, fiddles and banjos were central. Other early instruments included the cotton hoe, combs, and drinking glasses. Modern music often includes a wide range of instrumentation suitable for the specific dance style, such as the Two Step or West Coast Swing.
sections.costume_and_setting: The style is heavily influenced by the use of cowboy boots, which dictate the gliding, flat-footed movement. Historically, dances were held in large farmhouses, kitchens, town halls, or at ranch-based events. Modern venues range from small lounges to massive nightclubs like the former Gilley's Club.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically, dances were associated with communal work events called 'frolics.' They served as essential social gatherings for isolated frontier communities. Today, they remain social activities held in clubs, dance halls, and community centers.
sections.notable_figures: Skippy Blair is noted for her 1994 observation on the popularity of country dance. Bill C. Malone is cited as a music historian who described the early, mingled styles as a 'dance without a name.'
sections.regional_variants: Texas is known for 'kicker dancing.' West Texas ranch dances were large-scale community functions. Clogging is a distinct step dance associated with the Appalachian region and bluegrass music.
sections.lineage: The tradition descends from European reels, quadrilles, and cotillions, which were transformed by American frontier culture and African-American musical influences.

claims.text: Country–western dance encompasses any of the dance forms or styles which are typically danced to country-western music, and which are stylistically associated with American country and/or western traditions.
Because of cowboy boots, country western dance is more likely to feature a flat-footed glide with some heel and toe touches rather than a lot of 'toe type' dancing.
In frontier days men danced with each other when women were not available, with those taking the woman's role wearing handkerchiefs tied around one arm.
Country–western dance originated in the dances and music brought to the United States by the people of the British Isles and continental Europe.
Frolics were community events often associated with communal work such as corn shucking or house raising, where participants celebrated with a feast and dancing.
The tradition is considered a living practice, with various forms like the Two Step and Line Dance remaining popular in contemporary settings.

sections.origins_and_history: Modern line dance emerged in the 20th century, drawing on 19th-century European folk traditions and American physical education curricula. Key developments include the 1957 'Madison', the 1970s disco-era 'Electric Slide', and the 1990s country-western boom sparked by 'Achy Breaky Heart'.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers stand in parallel lines, repeating a fixed sequence of steps. Movements are performed individually without physical contact. Dancers rotate to face different 'walls' (front, back, sides) based on the specific choreography.
sections.music_and_instruments: Historically tied to country-western music, the genre now encompasses pop, disco, Latin, rock, and techno. Music is typically chosen for its steady, repetitive beat that aligns with the 32, 48, or 64-step sequences.
sections.costume_and_setting: While historically associated with western wear and boots, modern participants often wear casual clothing and specialized dance trainers. It is practiced in dance bars, social clubs, and sports centers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Line dance serves as a social activity and a recreational sport. It is used for community building in social clubs and as a structured exercise format in sports associations.
sections.notable_figures: Ric Silver (choreographer of the Electric Slide), Max Perry, Jo Thompson Szymanski, and Scott Blevins.
sections.regional_variants: Variations include contra-style (lines facing each other) and diverse regional adaptations of country-western, such as the 'Western Swing' and 'Honky Tonk' styles.
sections.lineage: Derived from European folk dances and 20th-century American show dance; influenced by ballroom, disco, and global pop music.

claims.text: A line dance is a choreographed dance in which a group of people dance along to a repeating sequence of steps while arranged in one or more lines or rows.
The Electric Slide, associated with the song 'Electric Boogie', was created in 1976.
Durham, N.C. was declared the line dancing capital of America in 2014.
In a four-wall dance, the direction faced at the end of the sequence is 90 degrees to the right or left of the direction faced at the beginning.
The Madison, a novelty dance created and first performed in Columbus, Ohio, in 1957, was one of the first true line dances.
Line dancing is a living tradition practiced in social clubs and dance bars worldwide.

sections.origins_and_history: The genre originated in the early 1990s in Chicago, Illinois, created by the Mexican immigrant community. While the name refers to the state of Durango, Mexico, the movement was solidified in the United States. Groups like Paraíso Tropical de Durango and Montéz de Durango were early pioneers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance, known as Pasito Duranguense, is performed to a fast 2/4 polka rhythm. It involves rhythmic, repetitive footwork designed to match the sharp, synthesized beats of the music. Technique not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Duranguense blends Tamborazo (saxophone, trombone, tambora) with Technobanda (electronic keyboards like Korg X3/N364/Yamaha DX7, drum set, vocals). It is played in a fast 2/4 polka meter.

claims.text: Duranguense is a subgenre of regional Mexican music that functions as a hybrid of Technobanda and Tamborazo.
The genre relies on specific instruments including the saxophone, trombone, tambora, and electronic keyboards like the Korg X3.
The genre's popularity peaked in the mid-to-late 2000s among Mexican and Mexican American communities.
Although named for the state of Durango, the genre was actually born in Chicago, Illinois.
The music is typically played in a fast 2/4 polka rhythm.
Conjunto Atardecer is recognized as a leading group within the genre.

claims.text: James Cronin founded Ceroc in London, England, holding the first event in January 1980 at Porchester Hall.
The name Ceroc is said to derive from the French phrase 'c'est le roc', meaning 'it is rock'.
Ceroc introduced taxi dancers in 1994 to assist beginners during classes.
Ceroc classes are structured with frequent partner rotation, allowing the organization to advertise that no partner is required.
Ceroc is a living tradition with more than 200 venues across the United Kingdom and franchises in Europe, Asia, Australia, and New Zealand.

claims.text: Go-go dancing originated in the early 1960s at the French bar Whisky a Gogo, located in the town of Juan-les-Pins.
On 19 June 1964, Carol Doda began go-go dancing topless at the Condor Club on Broadway and Columbus in the North Beach neighborhood of San Francisco.
In 1964, the Los Angeles–based club Whisky a Go Go began suspending go-go dancers above the audience in glass cages.
The term go-go derives from the phrase 'go-go-go' for a high-energy person, and was influenced by the French expression à gogo, meaning 'in abundance, galore'.
Many 1960s-era nightclub dancers wore short, fringed skirts and high boots which eventually came to be called go-go boots.

sections.origins_and_history: The Running Man emerged in the mid-1980s, with MC Hammer in Oakland, California, credited for its popularization. A proto-version was documented in 1978 during a Fela Kuti concert in Berlin.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dancer steps forward, then slides the front foot backward while moving fists horizontally in front of the body. It mimics the motion of a stationary runner.
sections.music_and_instruments: Typically performed to 1980s and 1990s hip-hop and pop music. The rhythm is usually a steady 4/4 beat that supports the repetitive nature of the sliding steps.

sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a party dance, it evolved into a performance staple for concerts and music videos. It serves as a display of rhythmic coordination and athletic style.

sections.regional_variants: The Roger Rabbit, popularized by Bobby Brown, is a variant that functions as a 'backwards' version of the Running Man.
sections.lineage: The Running Man is a core hip-hop dance that influenced the Melbourne shuffle and various novelty fad dances.

sections.origins_and_history: Throwouts are a variation of the Balboa swing dance, a style that emerged in the United States. The dance move is historically linked to the development of Balboa, which emphasizes close-embrace footwork and rapid, small-step rhythms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The move is typically initiated from a comearound. On counts 5-6, the lead releases their right arm, allowing the follower to move to arm's distance. On count 7, the lead begins a new variation. Specific variations include the swing out, outer turn, and follow shine, each involving specific footwork and timing adjustments on counts 7-8 and 1-4.

claims.text: Throwouts are variations of the swing dance Balboa and are also known as Toss-outs.
The main idea is that the follower moves to arm's distance from the lead.
On the 5–6, the lead lets go with his right arm, and the follow naturally moves apart.
In the swing out variation, on counts 7–8, the lead and follow both kick and hold.
In the outer turn variation, the lead brings the follow forward, but blocks on the 1, leading to an outer turn or double turn.
In the follow shine variation, the lead holds still on counts 7, 8, 1, and 2 and then does a comearound on 3.

sections.origins_and_history: The carnavalito is a pre-Hispanic dance of the Altiplano. It evolved through syncretism with Spanish colonial culture. In eastern Bolivia, it consolidated as a symbol of national integration after 1952.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers move in rows, wheels, or serpentine lines. A leader with a handkerchief directs the group. Common figures include 'el puente' (the bridge), 'las alas' (the wings), and 'las calles' (the streets).
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is typically in a minor pentatonic mode. Instruments include the quena, siku, charango, bombo, and caja chayera. In eastern Bolivia, guitars, maracas, and metallic instruments are used.
sections.costume_and_setting: In eastern Bolivia, women wear a colorful tipoy and flowers in their hair. Men wear white shirts, trousers, and a 'sombrero de Sao'. In the Andes, attire varies by local indigenous tradition.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is performed during religious festivities and community celebrations. It is a joyful, innocent, and communal activity, often serving as a game among participants.
sections.notable_figures: Raúl Otero Reiche and Jorge Luna (composers of 'Palomita de Arrozal'). Ariel Ramírez (composer of the 'Gloria' in Misa Criolla).
sections.regional_variants: Andean (Jujuy, Salta, Altiplano) vs. Eastern Bolivian (Santa Cruz, Beni, Pando). The latter is more akin to a light waltz or taquirari.
sections.lineage: Derived from indigenous Andean dance; shares roots with the huayno and is related to the taquirari.

sections.origins_and_history: Daggering emerged in Jamaica's dancehall scene and was named around 2006. The term describes a style of dance involving sexually explicit, simulated intercourse movements. It has roots in longstanding dancehall practices but gained distinct identity and popularity through music videos and artists promoting the style. The dance spread globally via YouTube.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Daggering is danced by male and female partners in close proximity, with the male typically thrusting his crotch into the female's buttocks or vice versa. Movements are frantic and energetic, simulating sexual acts. The dance is performed to dancehall music. Detailed footwork, rhythm patterns, and technique are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Daggering is performed to dancehall music. Artists associated with daggering music include Aidonia, Dexta Daps, Ding Dong, Major Lazer, Mavado, Mr. Vegas, Popcaan, Shenseea, Spice, and Vybz Kartel. The music typically features rhythmic beats suitable for vigorous dancing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Daggering is performed in dancehall settings such as clubs and parties where dancehall music is played. Costumes are typical of dancehall culture, often casual and revealing, supporting the dance's explicit nature.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Daggering is a social dance performed in dancehall parties and music video contexts. It is a form of erotic dance expressing sexuality and energy. The dance is controversial and banned from Jamaican broadcast media due to explicit content and health concerns.
sections.notable_figures: Artists linked to daggering music include Aidonia, Dexta Daps, Ding Dong, Major Lazer, Mavado, Mr. Vegas, Popcaan, Shenseea, Spice, and Vybz Kartel. Reggae historian David Katz noted the role of music videos in popularizing daggering.
sections.regional_variants: Daggering is specifically Jamaican and linked to dancehall culture. It is roughly equivalent to the Caribbean 'cabin stabbing' dance style but no detailed variants are described.
sections.lineage: Daggering descends from Jamaican dancehall dance traditions and is a recent development from around 2006. It is a form of erotic dance within the broader dancehall genre.

sections.origins_and_history: Janger originated in the 1920s in the village of Menyali, North Bali. It was created as a social dance, with songs derived from local horse drivers. Its name means 'infatuation' or being madly in love, reflecting its flirtatious nature.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance begins with a tableau vivant and a welcoming song. Twelve male dancers perform an elaborate kecak routine, then sit in two rows of six facing each other. A female group enters, singing traditional folk songs and performing a slower dance with fluid, undulating arm movements. The female dancers form two lines of six, while the male dancers form a boundary around the playing area. The performance continues with a drama usually about domestic themes. Technique details such as footwork and rhythm are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music includes traditional folk songs sung by the female group. The male dancers perform a kecak routine, which is a vocal chant-based performance. Specific instruments are not detailed in the sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costume and setting details are not described in the sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Janger is a social dance performed by youth groups, emphasizing flirtation and community interaction. The drama that follows often concerns domestic themes, reflecting social narratives.
sections.notable_figures: I Madé Kredek is noted for claiming the dance originated in Menyali village and for linking the songs to horse drivers in the area.
sections.regional_variants: Janger is performed by Balinese people in Bali and by the Osing people in eastern Java. No further regional variants are described.
sections.lineage: Janger is related to Balinese dance traditions and incorporates the kecak chant routine. It shares cultural ties with dances like Gandrung and Kecak.

claims.text: Janger is a traditional Balinese and Osing dance drama performance originated from the Indonesian island of Bali.
The term roughly translates to 'infatuation,' with a connotation of someone who is madly in love.
Janger is a social dance created in the 1920s, though its exact date of origin is unknown.
I Madé Kredek claims it originated in the village of Menyali, North Bali and the songs featured in it were those of the horse drivers in the area.
Janger is a 'flirtatious youth group dance' which begins with a tableau vivant and a welcoming song.
Twelve male dancers (kecak) perform an elaborate routine, then sit in two rows of six facing each other.
A female group enters, sings a traditional folk song, and performs a slower dance with an emphasis on fluid, undulating, arm movements.
The female dancers form two lines of six, with the male dancers forming a boundary around the playing area.
The opening is followed by a drama, which usually concerns some sort of domestic theme.
Janger is a living tradition performed by Balinese and Osing communities.

sections.origins_and_history: Emerging in the late 1960s, dangdut evolved from the Orkes Melayu and the heavy influence of Bollywood film music. It was popularized in the 1970s by figures like Rhoma Irama and Ellya Khadam.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dangdut is the name of the dance performed to the music, but specific footwork, gestures, and technical instruction are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features a 4/4 rhythm with a strong fourth-beat accent. Instruments include tabla, gendang, flute (suling), mandolin, guitars, sitar, drum machines, and synthesizers.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur on stages, in concert venues, and at family celebrations. Costume details are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Used in karaoke, family celebrations, government office exercise, and political campaigns. It serves as both popular entertainment and a medium for religious preaching.
sections.notable_figures: Rhoma Irama, Elvy Sukaesih, Inul Daratista, Mansyur S., Camelia Malik, Rita Sugiarto, Iyeth Bustami, Ayu Ting Ting, Lesti Kejora, and Via Vallen.
sections.regional_variants: Spiritual dangdut (preaching-focused) and koplo dangdut (faster-paced, often controversial).
sections.lineage: Derived from Orkes Melayu, Hindustani music, Arabic music, and various Indonesian regional folk styles.

claims.text: Dangdut is a genre of Indonesian folk music that is partly derived and fused from Hindustani, Arabic, and, to a lesser extent, Javanese, Malay, Minangkabau, Sundanese and local folk music.
The term dangdut is an onomatopoeia for the sound of the tabla (also known as gendang) drum, which is written dang and ndut.
Dangdut is also the name of the dance that one performs while listening to this music.
Musically, dangdut is characterized by a special rhythm in which the first beat of a 4/4 bar is light and the fourth beat is strongly emphasized.
The popularity of dangdut peaked in the 1970s and 1980s, but emerged in the late 1960s.
Dangdut remains an integral part of Indonesian life and pop culture despite conservative Muslim concerns over the supposed vulgarity of some performances.

sections.origins_and_history: The Siva Tau was composed during the 1980s to replace the traditional Maulu'ulu Moa. It was first performed in 1991 for the Rugby World Cup, intended to provide a more effective psychological boost for the players.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves military-style gestures. Performers mimic the handling of a spear, strike their knees, and challenge their opponents through direct, aggressive movements. The performance is accompanied by a vocal chant.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music consists of a vocal chant performed by the athletes. The lyrics are in the Samoan language.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed by teams in their respective sporting uniforms (rugby kits, wrestling attire) on the field or in the ring before a match or competition.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is performed before matches to express Samoan identity, pride, and dominance. It serves as a challenge to opponents and a psychological tool for the performers.
sections.notable_figures: The Usos (WWE performers) are noted for using the Siva Tau in their ring entrances.
sections.regional_variants: The Toa Samoa rugby league team uses a variant where 'Toa' replaces 'Manu' in the lyrics. The Manu Samoa team used a more aggressive version during the 2007 Rugby World Cup before reverting to the original.
sections.lineage: The Siva Tau is a descendant of traditional Polynesian war dances, replacing the Maulu'ulu Moa in the context of Samoan national sports.

basic_steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in a firm, grounded stance.
Mimic the motion of holding and thrusting a spear with the arms.
Perform rhythmic strikes to the knees or thighs to emphasize the beat.
Maintain a steady, aggressive vocal chant in unison with the group.
teaching.formation: Group formation, typically in a line or semi-circle facing the opposition.
teaching.level_notes: Focus on the intensity of the gesture and the unity of the group.

claims.text: The national rugby union team used to perform the traditional 'Maulu'ulu Moa' on tour.
Prior to the 1991 World Cup, the 'Manu' war chant was composed; it was considered more effective at psyching up players.
The Siva Tau is a Samoan dance performed by the Samoa rugby union and rugby league teams before each match.
The gestures are military and virile, including mimicking spear handling and striking the knees.
The national Australian rules football team performs the Siva Tau at its International Cup appearances.
In WWE, The Usos performed the Siva Tau as part of their ring entrance.
The Toa Samoa rugby league team also performs the Siva Tau with 'Toa' replacing 'Manu' in the lyrics.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is a 19th-century synthesis of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka and the Samoan Māuluulu.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers sit cross-legged, right leg over left. Gestures (haka) are performed close to the body, except in the Vavaʻu tradition.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompanied by the nafa, a 200-liter iron fuel drum with a leather skin, and vocal singing.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed on special occasions like weddings or royal birthdays. Dancers are arranged in rows, often tiered by social status.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Used to praise specific people or events. The dance is a communal effort involving months of practice.
sections.notable_figures: The chief Malukava is the only dancemaster permitted to stand in front of the dancers by tradition.
sections.regional_variants: The Vavaʻu tradition features wider arm movements; the ʻUiha tradition features men standing behind seated women.
sections.lineage: Direct successor of the Tongan ʻotuhaka.

claims.text: The māʻuluʻulu is a traditional Tongan dance, performed by a group of seated men and women.
Stylistically, the dance form is a direct successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka having been synthesized with the Samoan Māuluulu.
The performers sit down in a row on the ground, crosslegged, usually the right leg over the left.
The nafa-master can make a whole show of it, hitting the drums with his two decorated sticks almost performing a dance himself.
The lyrics of the song is usually made for the occasion, praising the object into the skies.
A māʻuluʻulu takes around 15 minutes to complete. But it may have taken the performers 2 or 3 months to memorise the sequence of gestures.
The ma'ulu'ulu is performed on special occasions, whether it be a birthday, a wedding it all depends on who is willing to do it.

claims.text: The Najdi Ardah is the most common variant of the ardah dance in Saudi Arabia.
The dance is performed by two rows of men facing each other.
The dance was inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2015.
The term ardah is thought to derive from the Arabic verb meaning to show or parade.
The dance was originally performed by tribal men before going to war.
The dance is accompanied by drums and spoken poetry.
The Saudi government officially renamed the dance 'Saudi Ardah' in the 21st century.

sections.origins_and_history: Mhande is a traditional Shona performance practice associated with the Karanga people of the Midlands, particularly the Shurugwi District. It is historically tied to the mutoro rain rituals and kurova guva ceremonies, serving as an embodiment of Karanga epistemology and cultural values.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in conjunction with music, utilizing rhythmic footwork accentuated by rattles worn on the legs. It involves stylized and coded movements that communicate historical and spiritual knowledge. The dance is integrated with singing and hand-clapping (makwa).
sections.music_and_instruments: The ensemble typically features two drummers using Shauro (call) and Tsinhiro (response) drums. Music is characterized by triple meter, cyclical structure, and polyrhythms, with a specific rhythmic pattern of '1, 2 … 1, 2, 3, 4 … 1, 2, 3.' Rattles and sometimes marimbas are also used.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur in both ceremonial and non-ceremonial settings, including the Matonjeni sanctuary in the Matopo Hills. Dancers wear rattles on their legs to accentuate the rhythm of their footwork.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Mhande is central to the mutoro rain ritual, where it serves as a prayer for rain, and kurova guva ceremonies. It is used to invoke majukwa rain spirits and ancestral spirits (dzavadzimu) to facilitate communication with the Creator, Mwari.

sections.regional_variants: Associated specifically with the Midlands tribes and the rural Karanga community of the Shurugwi District.
sections.lineage: A traditional Shona performance practice passed down through generations.

claims.text: Mhande is a traditional performance practiced among the Shona people, involving music and dance.
It is a vital element of the mutoro ceremony, an annual rain ritual of the Karanga.
The unique rhythmic pattern of '1, 2 … 1, 2, 3, 4 … 1, 2, 3' sets mhande apart from other ceremonial Shona musical and dance styles.
Most mhande performances involve two drummers, using Shauro and Tsinhiro drums, accompanied by hand clapping (makwa) from nearby participants.
The rhythms, songs, and dances serve as a medium for communicating with majukwa rain spirits, who convey their desires to the Creator, Musiki or Mwari, requesting rain.
Mhande is a living tradition passed down through generations.

sections.origins_and_history: The ritual originated in pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica, with evidence found in ceramics from the pre-Classic period in Nayarit. It is believed to have been created by the Nahua, Huastec, and Otomi peoples to appease gods during a severe drought. Following the Spanish Conquest, the ritual was suppressed, though it persisted through oral tradition and secret practice.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Five participants climb a 30-meter pole. The caporal remains at the top on a platform (manzana), playing a flute and drum. Four voladores sit on a frame (cuadro), wind ropes around the pole 13 times each, and then fall backward to descend in a spinning motion. The descent creates a moving pyramid shape until they reach the ground.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed by the caporal at the top of the pole using a one-handed flute and a small drum. The music is categorized into 'sones', which are specific to the ritual. The caporal plays to acknowledge the four cardinal directions and the sun.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditional Totonac dress includes red pants, a white shirt, a cloth across the chest symbolizing blood, and a cap adorned with flowers and mirrors. The mirrors represent the sun, and multicolored ribbons represent the rainbow. The pole, or 'palo volador', is a 30-meter structure that serves as the central setting.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The ritual is a fertility rite designed to bring rain and honor the gods. It is performed on patron saint feast days and at cultural festivals like the Cumbre Tajín. It symbolizes the connection between the sky, earth, and underworld.
sections.notable_figures: Jesús Arroyo Cerón was a prominent figure who trained women as voladores; he died in 2006 after a fall from a pole. His daughter, Isabel, was one of the first women he trained.
sections.regional_variants: Variations exist among the Nahua and Otomi, where there may be no dance before climbing. Some versions involve six dancers on a five-sided frame. In Guatemala, the ritual is performed in Joyabaj, Chichicastenango, and Cubulco.
sections.lineage: The ritual is considered a continuation of ancient Mesoamerican traditions, with modern practice heavily influenced by Totonac cultural preservation efforts in Veracruz.

claims.text: The ritual consists of dance and the climbing of a 30-meter pole from which four of the five participants then launch themselves.
The four ropes are each wound thirteen times for a total of fifty-two, the number of years in a Mesoamerican great year.
The ritual was named an Intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO in 2009.
The caporal stands on a capstan, called a manzana, at the top of the pole.
The four voladores represent the four cardinal directions as well as the four elements: earth, air, fire and water.
The ritual is associated with the Totonac people, especially those in and around Papantla in the Mexican state of Veracruz.
The ritual is a living tradition, though modified, in isolated pockets in Mexico.

sections.origins_and_history: The Ōte'a predates European contact in Tahiti, originally serving as a male-only dance. It was documented in 1928 by Teuira Henry as a violent, jerky war dance. The modern form was established in the second half of the 20th century through the Heiva i Tahiti festival.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers stand in rows and perform synchronized movements. Women focus on hip-shaking (fa'arapu), while men perform scissor-like leg movements (pa'oti). The dance includes 23 regulated steps for men in competition. Gestures are abstract but thematic.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is strictly percussion-based, featuring the tōʻere (slit log), the pahu (shark-skin drum), and the faʻatētē. There is no singing. The percussion ensemble itself is also called an 'otea'.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes typically include plant-fiber skirts (more), headpieces, and necklaces. Tassels are used to accentuate hip movement. Modern versions may use synthetic materials like polyester or reflective surfaces.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is a central feature of Tahitian cultural identity and is performed at festivals like the Heiva i Tahiti. It serves as a narrative medium, with gestures reenacting daily occupations, nature, or historical themes.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: The dance is performed in three forms: Ōte'a tāne (men), Ōte'a vahine (women), and Ōte'a ʻāmui (mixed).
sections.lineage: It is a form of 'ori tahiti, sharing roots with other traditional Tahitian dances, though distinct from the melodic aparima.

claims.text: The ʻōteʻa is a traditional dance and accompanying music from Tahiti characterized by a rapid hip-shaking motion to percussion accompaniment.
The dance is performed in three forms: by men (tāne), by women (vahine), or by both genders (ʻāmui).
The dance relies exclusively on drum accompaniment, including the tōʻere, pahu, and faʻatētē.
The dance was historically a male-only war dance, described in 1928 as violent and jerky.
The modern form of the dance was fixed during the second half of the 20th century through dance competitions.
The Ōte'a is a living tradition performed today.

claims.text: Sean-nós dance is an informal, spontaneous, solo form of dance.
The dance is characterized by low-to-the-ground footwork and a percussive battering step.
Sean-nós dance has influenced American vernacular solo dance forms including flat-footing and buck dancing.
The interaction between the African banjo and European fiddle influenced the music to which older American dancers moved.
Small communities of sean-nós dancers exist in cities like Boston, Philadelphia, and Portland.
The dance is a living tradition maintained by teachers who learned in the west of Ireland.

sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves the imitation of the labi-labi's movements. Dancers use exaggerated facial expressions and humorous physical actions to entertain the audience. claims.text: The earliest Labi-labi dance was detected and originated in Kampung Sarang Tiong, Endau, Kuala Rompin, Pahang.
This dance has been danced since the 1950s.
The Labi-labi dance in Kampung Sarang Tiong is inspired and developed by individuals who are skilled in martial arts.
Labi-labi dance in Kampung Sarang Tiong was inspired by the incident of a wife (Ms. Siti) who craved to eat labi-labi.
The Labi-Labi Dance in Kampung Pulau Rumput, Pekan, Pahang was brought by Encik Iderus bin Ginuh from Kampung Alai, Rompin to Pekan, Pahang in 1964.
The Labi-Labi dance in Kampung Jambu, Pekan is based on the experience of a fisherman named Pak Ngah Hitam in Endau, Kuala Rompin who was stunned by the movement of labi-labi.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated between the 1st century BC and 7th century AD, with early depictions found in Goguryeo wall paintings. It was later codified as a military ritual in Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnamdo, and gained prominence under Admiral Yi Sun-shin during the Imjin War.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in two parts: a drum dance and a sword dance. The drum dance involves four primary dancers and up to twelve others, while the sword dance features four women using two swords and long sleeves (Hansam). The movement is defined by a pattern of three-advances and three-retreats.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided by an orchestra playing pieces from the Yeongsan Hoisang repertoire, specifically Samhyeun Dodeuri and Taryeong. The primary instrument is the large drum, which features a taeguk pattern.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear flower hats for the drum dance and archery cloths for the sword dance. The performance space is centered around a large drum, and the dancers utilize Hansam (long sleeves) to accentuate their movements.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally performed to wish for victory in war and to reward soldiers, it is now performed at memorial services honoring Admiral Yi Sun-shin in the spring and autumn.
sections.notable_figures: Admiral Yi Sun-shin is the central historical figure associated with the dance's military application.
sections.regional_variants: The tradition is specifically handed down from Tongyeong, Gyeongsangnamdo.
sections.lineage: The dance shares origins with the Mugo of the Royal Court, both dating back to the Goryeo dynasty under King Chungnyeol.

In the sword dance or geommu (검무), the sword is used to absorb energy from the heavens and purify the Seungjeonmu ritual.

sections.origins_and_history: Pendet originated as a floral offering ritual dance performed in Balinese Hindu temples to welcome gods descending from khayangan. It was initially part of piodalan ceremonies and symbolized gratitude and respect. In the 1950s, I Wayan Rindi and Ni Ketut Reneng codified the dance with four dancers for tourism shows in Denpasar. In 1961, I Wayan Beratha expanded it to five dancers, and in 1962 he organized a mass performance with 800 dancers at the Asian Games opening in Jakarta.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Pendet is performed by 4-5 young girls carrying small silver bowls decorated with young palm leaves, filled with flower petals and incense. The dancers move from shrine to shrine within temple yards, sprinkling petals to welcome gods and guests. Movements are simple, foundational Balinese dance steps learned by imitation, suitable for beginners. The dance may be performed intermittently during temple feasts and social events.
sections.music_and_instruments: not described in sources
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional Balinese attire suitable for temple ceremonies. Each carries a small silver bowl decorated with yellow janur (young palm leaves) containing flower petals and incense. The setting is primarily temple courtyards but also includes social and tourist venues.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Pendet is performed during temple ceremonies (piodalan), social events, and tourism shows. It symbolizes welcoming gods, spirits, and guests, expressing gratitude, respect, and joy. The dance is a form of Bebalihan (entertainment dance) rather than a sacred Wali dance.
sections.notable_figures: I Wayan Rindi and Ni Ketut Reneng codified the dance in the 1950s. I Wayan Beratha expanded the choreography and scale in the 1960s, including the mass performance at the 1962 Asian Games.

claims.text: Pendet dance is a traditional dance from Bali, Indonesia, in which floral offerings are made to purify the temple or theater as a prelude to ceremonies or other dances.
Pendet is typically performed by young girls, carrying bowls of flower petals, handfuls of which are cast into the air at various times in the dance.
The choreography, movements, costumes and properties were codified by two artists from Sumertha village, Denpasar; I Wayan Rindi and Ni Ketut Reneng in the 1950s.
In 1961, I Wayan Beratha developed this dance and increased the number of dancers to five, as is often performed now.
In 1962, I Wayan Beratha and his colleagues developed Pendet dance as a mass dance with no less than 800 dancers, featured in the opening ceremony of the Asian Games in Jakarta.
Pendet is considered a form of Bebalihan, often performed secularly to welcome guests or audiences.
Pendet may be danced by anyone, taught simply by imitation, and does not require arduous training.
The original Pendet dance is performed by 4-5 young pre-pubescent girls in the yards of Balinese Hindu temples.

sections.origins_and_history: The Serpentine dance was created by Loïe Fuller in 1892 at the Park Theatre in Brooklyn, New York. It evolved from the skirt dance, a burlesque form reacting against classical ballet, incorporating folk and popular dance elements. Fuller discovered the dance's visual potential accidentally when stage lights illuminated her large silk costume, inspiring her to develop the choreography around fabric movement and light effects. She patented her costume and lighting innovations and toured Europe from 1894, performing at venues such as the Folies Bergère in Paris. The dance became emblematic of the Belle Époque’s artistic and technological enthusiasm.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dancer holds long silk skirts attached to rods concealed within the fabric, manipulating them with arm movements to create flowing waves, spirals, and billowing shapes. The choreography emphasizes graceful, continuous arm motions rather than footwork, with the dancer’s form often obscured by the fabric. The tempo is moderate to slow, allowing the fabric to respond fluidly to movement and colored lighting. Technique details such as footwork and rhythm are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: not described in sources
sections.costume_and_setting: The costume consists of hundreds of yards of lightweight China silk sewn into a large conical skirt, attached to the dancer’s shoulders or head. Aluminum rods sewn invisibly into the fabric extend the dancer’s arms, allowing her to manipulate the silk expansively. The dance is performed on stage with multi-colored lighting designed by Fuller to project onto the silk, creating shifting patterns and illusions of fire, flowers, and butterflies. The setting is theatrical, often in vaudeville or variety theaters and early film studios.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Serpentine dance was primarily a stage performance intended to showcase the interplay of light, fabric, and movement. It symbolized natural elements like wind, water, flowers, and animals, aligning with Art Nouveau aesthetics. It marked a break from classical ballet’s focus on footwork, emphasizing 'dance libre' and abstraction. The dance was a popular entertainment form in the 1890s and early 1900s, performed in theaters and early cinema, reflecting contemporary fascination with technological progress and artistic innovation.
sections.notable_figures: Loïe Fuller, the creator and principal performer of the Serpentine dance, is the central figure. Other notable performers include Annabelle Moore, who popularized the dance in early films produced by Edison Studios. Minnie Renwood was an early imitator who replaced Fuller in some performances. The Lumière brothers and Georges Méliès produced film versions of the dance.
sections.regional_variants: not described in sources
sections.lineage: The Serpentine dance evolved from the skirt dance, itself a reaction against academic ballet and influenced by folk and popular dances like the can-can. It influenced later performance traditions involving large silk veils or wings, such as the Isis wings in belly dance. It also contributed to the development of modern dance and theatrical lighting techniques.

claims.text: The serpentine dance is a form of dance that was popular throughout the United States and Europe in the 1890s, becoming a staple of stage shows and early film.
The serpentine dance was originated by Loïe Fuller, who gave varying accounts of how she developed it.

The costume for her Serpentine Dance consisted of hundreds of yards of China silk which she let billow around her while lighting effects suggested that it was catching fire and taking shapes reminiscent of flowers, clouds, birds, and butterflies.
La danse serpentine est une chorégraphie créée par la danseuse américaine Loïe Fuller au Park Theatre de Brooklyn, à New York, le 15 février 1892.
Loïe Fuller dépose quatre brevets pour protéger ses créations : systèmes de miroirs qui reproduisent à l’infini ses mouvements, baguettes à pointe courbe, etc.

Loïe Fuller, die Erfinderin des Serpentinentanz und „Fee de l’Electricité“, experimentierte mit farbigen Lichteffekten und Fotografien, die sie während ihres Tanzes auf ihr Schleierkostüm projizieren ließ.
The Serpentine dance was a frequent subject of early motion pictures, as it highlighted the new medium's ability to portray movement and light.
When the first films for the Kinetoscope were made in 1893, Thomas Edison invited Loie Fuller to perform but she refused to be filmed, leading to many imitators being filmed instead.

sections.origins_and_history: The Sigalegale puppet dance originates from the Batak Toba people of Samosir Island, Northern Sumatra, Indonesia. It is linked to a local legend about Nai Manggale, a childless woman who instructed her husband to create a lifesize puppet of herself to prevent her spirit from cursing him after death. Early 20th-century missionary Johannes Warneck described the use of the puppet in funerary ceremonies for wealthy men who died without heirs. The dance serves as a substitute for childless deceased persons, allowing their spirits to be honored and appeased.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Sigalegale puppet is mounted on a wheeled wooden platform and manipulated from behind by strings running through the platform. This allows the puppet's arms, body, and head to move, simulating dancing and crying. The puppet dances alongside the deceased's relatives, who also dance and weep. The dance is part of the papurpur sapata funerary ceremony. Technique details such as specific footwork or rhythm are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: not described in sources
sections.costume_and_setting: The Sigalegale puppet is dressed in traditional Batak costume, including a shawl, headdress, and gold jewelry. The puppet is life-sized and mounted on a large wheeled platform. The setting is a funerary ceremony on Samosir Island, often held outdoors in the village, including a procession to the market where meat is distributed.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Sigalegale dance is performed during papurpur sapata funerary ceremonies for persons of high rank who died without offspring. It serves to dispel the curse of dying childless and to placate the spirit of the deceased. The puppet acts as a symbolic child to perform funerary rites, ensuring the deceased's spirit is honored and does no harm to the community.

claims.text: Sigalegale is a wooden puppet used in a funeral dance performance of the Batak people in Samosir Island, Northern Sumatra.
The puppet is operated from behind using strings that run through the ornate wooden platform on which it stands.
Traditionally the performance was carried out for childless persons as a substitute to perform funerary rites.
Complicated Sigalegale puppets could be life sized and featured actuation using wet moss or sponges to simulate crying.
The puppets were mounted on wheeled platforms and danced during funerary ceremonies called papurpur sapata.
The ritual dispelled the curse of dying childless and placated the spirit of the deceased.
The use of the Sigalegale figure originated from the legend of Nai Manggale, a childless woman who instructed her husband to create the puppet.
Early 20th century German missionary Johannes Warneck described the puppet's use in funerary ceremonies.
The puppet was clothed in traditional costume with shawl, headdress, and gold jewelry.
The puppet was led to the market where meat was distributed among those gathered.

sections.origins_and_history: Inai dance originates from the Malay court tradition and is performed during the circumcision ceremonies of palace children. It is popular in Perlis, northern Kedah, and Kelantan. Historically, it was performed by two men and is linked to significant palace events such as weddings, coronations, and circumcisions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features continuous circular movements with intricate finger and hand gestures. It combines movements from Mak Yong, Silat, and acrobatic bending, where the dancer bends backward facing the floor. Traditionally performed by two men, the Perak variant is performed by palace maids in a garden setting. Technique not described in sources in detail.
sections.music_and_instruments: Inai dance is accompanied by Gendang Terinai, playing three songs: Temang Welo, Selong, and Mak Inang. The Perak variant uses drums, gongs, and flutes. The music is rhythmic and ceremonial, supporting the dance's formal nature.

It is presented to these children as they are about to be circumcised and sit on the throne.
Inai dance is popular in Perlis, northern Kedah, and Kelantan.
It has a combination of dance movements found in Mak Yong, Silat and acrobatic positions known as bending.
In the past, this dance was performed by two men.
There is another Inai Dance from Perak that is danced by the palace maids in the flower garden.
The main musical instruments are drums, gongs, and flutes.
Inai dance is also accompanied by the beat of Gendang Terinai by playing three songs, namely Temang Welo, Selong and Mak Inang.
It is still played at regular wedding ceremonies.

sections.origins_and_history: The passamezzo originated in 16th-century Italy and was popular through the early 17th century. It was known throughout Europe, with early printed collections appearing in Germany, Italy, France, and England. The dance is closely related to the pavane, sometimes considered a faster variant or an elaborated form. By the late 16th century, the passamezzo gradually replaced the pavane in popularity. It was typically performed in suites with faster triple-time dances like the saltarello or galliard. The name's origin is uncertain, possibly referring to its tempo or a 'step and a half' figure. The dance disappeared around 1640.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. Historical sources suggest the passamezzo involved variations on pavane steps with galliard-like movements, danced by couples in a procession or courtly setting. The dance was in binary rhythm and performed at a measured, steady tempo. It was often followed by triple-time dances such as the saltarello.
sections.music_and_instruments: The passamezzo is defined by two main chord progressions: passamezzo antico (minor key) and passamezzo moderno (major key). These progressions form ostinato bass lines repeated throughout the dance. The passamezzo antico progression is i – VII – i – V – III – VII – i – V – I, while the moderno is I – IV – I – V – I – IV – I – V – I. Instruments commonly included lute, keyboard, and ensemble settings. Vocal examples exist but are rare. The music is calm and measured, with fluid rhythmic movement supporting the dance steps.
