sections.origins_and_history: Wari originates from the district of Huari in Peru's Áncash region, rooted in a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita celebrating the first rains. It evolved through syncretism with Spanish colonial religious festivals like the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary. The dance was recorded in 1570 by Cristóbal de Molina as Waritaki, reflecting its cultural transformation. Variants exist in Pomabamba and other northern towns with distinct choreography and tempo.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians, sometimes eight dancers plus a captain in urban areas. The choreography has three main moments: circular formations with rhythmic support on the fourth beat, a light step called arrebato, and a strong zapateo foot stamping ending the dance. Dancers move in circles, emphasizing rhythmic footwork and coordinated group patterns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is played by two cajeros using the pinkullo flute and wanqar drum. The pinkullo is a wooden flute with four holes played with the left hand, made from waroma wood. The wanqar is a large eucalyptus bark drum carried on the left shoulder and struck with a stick. The music follows traditional patterns, with chuscadas played during general dances, a regional huayno variant.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear formal blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, covered by floral shawls tied across the chest. Embroidered velvet sashes with golden threads are worn at the waist. The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño, and the face with a pink mesh mask painted with facial features. Hats are white toquilla straw with colored ribbons and artificial flower crowns. Knee pads with 35-40 bells symbolize penitence. White gloves and a command baton with a dog head and leather whip complete the attire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during the Virgin of the Rosary festival, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in Huari, and occasionally the Virgin of the Assumption in Chacas. The dance marks the agricultural cycle's start of rains and reflects syncretism between indigenous and Christian traditions, embodying devotion and penitence.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: Variants exist in Pomabamba province and towns like Sihuas, Urpay, Taurija, and Pataz, differing in choreography and musical tempo from the Huari version.
sections.lineage: Descended from pre-Inca agricultural dances linked to the pocoy mita festival, evolving through Spanish colonial influence and Christian religious festivals into the current Wari dance.

claims.text: La huaridanza, también llamada danza de los caballeros de Huari, es una danza ritual de origen mestizo andino-español, originario del distrito de Huari, en el departamento peruano de Áncash.
Su origen se remonta al período del sincretismo inca y español a partir de una danza mucho más antigua, posiblemente de origen preinca.
En 1570, el cronista Cristóbal de Molina detalla que la danza tenía como nombre Waritaki, esta evolucionó a medida que la nueva cultura española se consolidaba en la región.
Está compuesta tradicionalmente de cuatro danzantes y dos músicos de flauta y tambor llamados cajeros.

La coreografía de la huaridanza tiene tres 'momentos' fundamentales, en que los danzantes hacen el recorrido formando círculos, con la apoyatura rítmica en el cuarto compás, el arrebato, que es un paso ligero, y el jaleo o zapateo, con un paso fuerte a modo de fuga de huayno.
El traje base es una vestimenta formal compuesta por un conjunto de terno azul o negro, camisa blanca y corbata, cubierto por un pañolón de tela floreada y con flecos.
Las rodilleras de pana, ricamente bordadas, tienen hileras de 35 a 40 cascabeles cada una, cuyo gran peso es entendido como una forma de penitencia.
La música es interpretada por dos músicos llamados cajeros, que portan un pinkullo, flauta de madera, y una caja o wanqar, tambor membranófono.

Las tonadas que se interpretan siguen un patrón tradicional durante la mayor parte del desempeño de la cuadrilla; solamente en las ocasiones en que se invita a un baile general se interpretan chuscadas.

Se presentan durante las festividades de la Virgen del Rosario, patrona de la ciudad de Huari en la exaltación de la cruz del mismo pueblo y, ocasionalmente, en la fiesta de la Virgen de la Asunción de Chacas.

sections.origins_and_history: Siguiriyas dates back to the late 18th century as part of the cante jondo tradition in Andalusia, with origins firmly rooted in Romani (Calé) culture. Early forms were performed a cappella like tonás, later developing guitar accompaniment. Key historical figures like the 19th-century cantaor El Planeta and his disciple El Fillo shaped its early classics, while the 1922 Concurso de Cante Jondo in Granada helped preserve its archaic forms through performers like El Tenazas and Manolo Caracol.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Introduced by Vicente Escudero in 1940, the dance is solemn, ceremonious, and pausado, lacking external ornamentation. The formal progression moves from a guitar and singer introduction to an entrada, initial letra, escobilla, second letra, danced falseta, and a final escobilla. Footwork and counter-rhythms interlock with the compás.
sections.music_and_instruments: Played in A Phrygian with a 12-count compás featuring accents on beats 1, 3, 5, 8, and 11. It utilizes guitar, palmas, and dancer footwork. Vocals feature heavy melismatic expression, notably the 'Ay' introduction, and follow a flexible verse structure (traditionally 6-6-11-6 syllables). Rubato and tempo shifts are heavily employed for dramatic effect.
sections.costume_and_setting: Not described in detail in the sources, though historically associated with intimate performance settings, traditional cafés cantantes, and wake gatherings (baile de velorio).
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Embodying the quintessence of jondura and cante puro, siguiriyas addresses profound human suffering, tragic love, imprisonment, and death. Historically linked to wake settings and serious artistic presentations.
sections.notable_figures: El Planeta (credited with the oldest style), El Fillo, Frasco el Colorao, La Niña de los Peines, Vicente Escudero (who introduced the dance in 1940), Paco La Luz, Silverio Franconetti, Diego Bermúdez Cala ('El Tenazas'), and Manolo Caracol.
sections.regional_variants: Variants differ across Andalusian regions: Cádiz features simple, unornamented styles (El Planeta), while Triana offers highly ornate interpretations (Frasco el Colorao, La Niña de los Peines). Related styles governed by the same compás include serranas, livianas, and cabales (major-key siguiriyas).
sections.lineage: Derived from primitive tonás. It forms part of the core cante jondo alongside soleares and tientos, and shares rhythmic frameworks with serranas and livianas.

sections.origins_and_history: Yangju byeolsandae nori was started by government officials working in Yangju province after a group of entertainers called Ttakttakyipae from Hanyang frequently broke their promise to perform. Lee Eul-chuk was the main organiser and first to produce mask dramas in Yangju, leveraging the town's status as a transport hub and administrative center. It traces lineage back to sandae gabhee, a welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats, and previously spread to regions like Aeohgae, Manrijae, Gameundol, Nokbeon, Sajikgol, Gupabal, Nodes, Toegyewon, and Uijeongbu.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance is organized primarily around dancing, miming, and drama with actors executing set lines in prose. The dance style is divided into geodeureumsik and kkaekkisik. Some character roles rely entirely on dancing and gestures without spoken words, while others combine dialogue with movement.
sections.music_and_instruments: The main instruments used in the performance are two piri flutes, one jeotdae, one haegeum, one janggu drum, and one buk drum. A kkwaenggari gong is added when needed, and performances occasionally rely solely on the piri and janggu. Musicians utilize the traditional rhythms of taryong or gutgurigok.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances took place at Sagikgol, north of Mount Bulgok, near a shaman house where props were stored. The production features thirty-two traditional characters, but because some masks are utilized in multiple roles, only twenty-two masks are worn during the performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed primarily in April, May, July, and August, as well as during rain-praying ceremonies. It begins with a ritual ceremony praying for a good performance where traditional foods like jora, tteok, colored fruits, a beef head, and a pork leg are served. Costs were traditionally covered by rich locals and merchants, while performers were unpaid.
sections.notable_figures: Lee Eul-chuk is recorded as the main organiser of the show and the first to produce mask dramas in Yangju.
sections.regional_variants: The tradition spread mainly from Seoul and Gyeonggi Province to Aeohgae, Manrijae, Gameundol, Nokbeon, Sajikgol, Gupabal, Nodes, Toegyewon and Uijeongbu, though it is no longer performed in these external regions.
sections.lineage: Originated from sandae gabhee, a welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats, and is also called sandi nori, sanji nori, or sandu nori.

sections.origins_and_history: The hand jive was invented in 1957 at The Cat's Whisker coffee bar in Soho, London, by Leon Bell. It was documented by Ken Russell, who observed that the dance was a necessity due to the lack of floor space for foot-based dancing.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves a sequence of hand and arm movements performed while standing or sitting. Key movements include thigh slapping, crossing the wrists, fist pounding, hand clapping, and hitchhike gestures.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is primarily associated with 1950s rhythm and blues, specifically the Bo Diddley beat. Notable tracks include 'Willie and the Hand Jive' by Johnny Otis and 'Born to Hand Jive' from the musical Grease.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance was born in 1950s coffee bars and is typically performed in casual, everyday attire. No specific costume is required.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a social dance for teenagers in crowded venues, it has since been used in theatrical performances, movies, and as a participatory activity in stage shows.

claims.text: In 1957, when filmmaker Ken Russell was a freelance photographer, he recorded the teenagers of Soho, London, hand-jiving in the basement of The Cat's Whisker coffee bar.
The hand jive is a dance particularly associated with music from the 1950s, rhythm and blues in particular.
It involves a complicated pattern of hand moves and claps at various parts of the body.
Hand moves include thigh slapping, crossing the wrists, fist pounding, hand clapping, and hitchhike moves.
The hand jive was popularized in the United States by Johnny Otis's 'Willie and the Hand Jive', described as a 'funky blues rendition in a Bo Diddley styling'.
The dance also went by the much more risque name 'hand job', but the title was changed as Grease was aimed at a family audience.

sections.origins_and_history: Traditional square dance descends from 18th-century cotillions and 19th-century quadrilles brought by settlers. It encompasses pre-1950 regional styles across North America, evolving through Northeastern, Southeastern, and Western branches.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced using a limited number of basic movements or 'calls' that enable average dancers to join by assimilation rather than formal lessons. Figures are executed in set orders or chosen from local repertoires by a prompter or caller, with regional variations appearing primarily in hand and arm positions.
sections.music_and_instruments: Danced almost exclusively to live music derived from Scottish and Irish jigs in 6/8 time and reels in 2/4 time. Fiddles serve as the primary lead instrument, supported regionally by pianos in New England, banjos and guitars in the South, double basses, accordions in Quebec and Newfoundland, and hammered dulcimers in Michigan.
sections.costume_and_setting: Events take place in community spaces, local halls, or revival venues. Dancers wear casual attire or dress up slightly, without requiring standardized square-dance-specific costumes.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Functioning as community gatherings, survival dances are sponsored by local churches, fire departments, or Granges where attendees mostly know one another. Revival dances and fun nights open the floor to the public with casual attire and frequent partner changes.
sections.notable_figures: Ted Sannella, Lloyd Shaw, and George Wade.
sections.regional_variants: Classified into Northeastern, Southeastern, and Western types, with documented roots across New England, the southern Appalachian Mountains, the Ozarks, and eastern Canada.
sections.lineage: Descended from the 18th-century cotillion and the 19th-century quadrille; serves as the precursor to modern Western square dance.

sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed with smooth, circular strokes and small lateral steps. It follows a three-part structure, alternating between active movements and 'syzme' (floating steps) and 'khyrdalyk' (small side-to-side movements).

sections.costume_and_setting: Traditionally performed by women at weddings, following the solemn dances of the matchmaker, parents, and groom.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance symbolizes the metaphor of a bride being taken from her family home, marking a transition in her life.
sections.notable_figures: Tamara Stepanovna Tkachenko (ethnographer) and Srbuhi Lisitsian (Armenian ethnographer).
sections.regional_variants: The dance is performed in both Armenia and Azerbaijan with variations in interpretation and emphasis on specific steps like 'syzme'.

claims.text: Uzundara is a lyrical Armenian and Azerbaijani dance traditionally performed by women.
The dance is associated with the Uzundere valley in the Karabakh region.

sections.origins_and_history: St. Louis Shag originated in St. Louis, Missouri, in the 1930s. It evolved from a combination of Lindy Hop, Collegiate Shag, and Charleston. The dance has maintained its characteristics through shifts in musical styles, including the transition from swing to rock and roll, jump blues, and R&B.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a closed position with a stationary 8-count basic. Common variations include the triple-step, kick, triple-step, kick pattern; the Kenny Wetzel version (triple-step, kick, step-stomp, run-run); and the Eddie Plunkett and Dottie Spokesfield version (triple-step, kick, double kick). Dancers often incorporate inside crosses, fall off the logs, and various stomps, kicks, and taps.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to up-tempo swing, rock and roll, jump blues, and boogie-woogie music. The music is characterized by strong, driving rhythms that support the percussive nature of the footwork.

claims.text: St. Louis Shag is a territory swing dance which originated in St. Louis, Missouri in the 1930s.
The dance has a stationary 8-count basic that is commonly composed of triple-step, kick, triple-step, kick.
Another basic version, popularized by Kenny Wetzel, an East St. Louis native who moved to Southern California in the 1950s, is composed of triple-step, kick, step-stomp, run-run.
Eddie Plunkett and Dottie Spokesfield of St. Louis had another version of the basic composed of triple-step, kick, double kick.
The dance's rhythmic variations include inside crosses (also known as over the tops), fall off the logs, and customizable stomps, kicks, taps, and holds.
St. Louis shag is a swing dance that evolved from the Lindy Hop, Collegiate Shag and Charleston.

sections.origins_and_history: Dance in Iran has been documented since the 6th millennium BC through archaeological artifacts. Ancient traditions included the worship of Mithra, which involved ritual sacrifice and movement to promote vigor. Throughout history, the tradition has been influenced by Greek, Arab, and Mongol occupations, leading to a slow disappearance of some heritage forms. The 1979 Revolution significantly altered the landscape of dance, leading to its prohibition in public spaces and the emigration of many professional dancers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Styles vary by genre. Chain dances involve group coordination, often in circles or lines, with an emphasis on footwork. Solo improvisational dance, common in social settings, utilizes delicate wrist circles, fluid arm movements, and expressive facial gestures. In some regional dances, such as those of the Baluchi people, dancers maintain rhythm by striking metal bracelets together. Technique not described in sources for specific step-by-step pedagogical sequences.
sections.music_and_instruments: The most common rhythm is 6/8, referred to as 'shir-e mâdar' (mother's milk). Variations exist, such as the 7/8 meter found in Motrebi styles. Music is central to all forms, from the rhythmic clapping in Baluchi 'chaap' dances to the instrumental accompaniment of traditional ensembles.
sections.costume_and_setting: Classical court dances feature rich silks, brocades, and flowing long skirts. Folk dancers often wear traditional ethnic clothing specific to their region, such as the colorful attire of the Basseri tribe. Performances occur in diverse settings, from private homes and weddings to traditional gymnasiums (zurkhaneh) and theatrical spaces.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dance is integral to social events, rites of passage, and religious ceremonies. It serves as a form of celebration, a tool for spiritual healing (as in the 'le’b guati' exorcism rituals), and a method of physical training for warriors.
sections.notable_figures: Jamileh (belly dancer), Farzaneh Kaboli (actress and dancer), Mohammad Khordadian, Shahrokh Moshkin-Ghalam, and Azita Sahebjam.
sections.regional_variants: Styles are highly regional. Examples include the Gilaki rice-harvesting dance (Qasemabadi), the Azerbaijani Yalli, the Baluchi Chaap, and the Bojnordi dance of the Turkic people in northeastern Iran.
sections.lineage: The tradition is a composite of ancient indigenous practices, influenced by regional ethnic groups and historical courtly refinements.

claims.text: The people of the Iranian plateau have known dance in the forms of music, play, drama or religious rituals and have used instruments like mask, costumes of animals or plants, and musical instruments for rhythm, at least since the 6th millennium BC.
The earliest researched dance from historic Iran is a dance worshiping Mithra in which a bull was sacrificed.
After the Iranian Revolution in 1979 dancing was no longer allowed due to its frequent mixing of the sexes.
Iran has four categories of dance: chain or line dances, solo improvisational dance, war or combat dances and ritual or spiritual dances.
The most common rhythm used for dance in Iran is the 6/8, to which one refers by the term shir-e mâdar.
The tradition of Iranian dance is a living practice, often performed in private settings.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is associated with the 1746 Act of Proscription, which banned traditional Highland dress. The name 'Seann Triubhas' translates to 'old trousers'. While popular legend links the first steps to the act of kicking off restrictive breeches, researchers like D. G. MacLennan have clarified that these steps were later additions to the tradition. The dance was historically taught by dancing masters in the 19th century and was performed in various footwear, including slippers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in either a '3 & 1' or '4 & 2' step configuration. The dance begins with a mandatory first step, followed by a series of slow, brushing movements. Upon a signal from the dancer, the music accelerates into a 'Quick Time' section, which features steps similar to the Highland Fling. The RSOBHD sets specific step requirements for championship competitions.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to the tune 'Whistle O'er the Lave o't'. Historically, it was played on the fiddle, but it is now standard to perform it to bagpipe music. The music requires a tempo shift from 94–104 bpm for the slow section to 112–124 bpm for the quick section.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear the standard Highland kilt outfit. Historically, the dance was performed in tartan trews, and in the 19th century, it was sometimes performed in regular shoes with heels.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is a primary event in global Highland dance competitions and is a standard requirement for dance theory exams. It serves as a cultural expression of the Highland identity and the historical struggle against the suppression of traditional dress.
sections.notable_figures: D. G. MacLennan, Elizabeth Grant, Margaret Gillis, Frank Rhodes, G. Douglas Taylor, William Cameron, Joan & Tom Flett.
sections.regional_variants: A percussive version was documented in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, by Frank Rhodes in 1957, which could be danced to the 'Irish Washerwoman' jig.
sections.lineage: The dance is a recognized form of Scottish Highland dance, sharing technical elements with the Highland Fling.

sections.origins_and_history: The polka-mazurka originated in the 1850s, with Johann Strauss II's 'La Viennoise' (1854) cited as the first example by the Strauss family. It was widely adopted in European salons as a cross-cultural variant of the polka, influenced by the French-polka and the schnell-polka.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in 3/4 time, with a step sequence spanning two measures (six counts). It involves a glide to the second position, a draw to the first, and a hop, with the lady mirroring the cavalier's movements in reverse. It is typically danced in a waltz-like rotation or in a straight line.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is written in 3/4 time, emphasizing the first beat of the bar. It typically features a main theme followed by a subsidiary theme and a free-style 'trio' section. Composers like Josef Strauss used the form to express romanticism and sensitivity.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance was performed in 19th-century European salons, requiring the formal attire typical of the era's 'gens du monde' (people of the world).
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It was a social ballroom dance, valued for its elegance and ability to express romantic sentiment. It was often performed in public and private social gatherings.
sections.notable_figures: Johann Strauss II, Josef Strauss, and Eduard Strauss are the most prominent composers associated with the genre.
sections.regional_variants: The dance shares characteristics with the Polish mazurka and the Nordic polska, though it remains distinct in its specific step-combination and ballroom application.
sections.lineage: It is a hybrid form, subclassed under both the polka and the mazurka, with influences from the French-polka and the schnell-polka.

claims.text: The polka-mazurka is a dance, musically similar to the mazurka, but danced much like the polka.
The first polka-mazurka example written by the Strauss family was in the year 1854 by Johann Strauss II, entitled La Viennoise op. 144.
Its tempo of 3 beats to the bar (3/4 time) meant that it was similar in rhythm to the waltz, but the emphasis of the polka-mazurka was on the first beat of the bar.
The dance is composed of one Mazurka and one Polka step, counting three to each step—six in all—taking two measures of music.
The Redowa or Pas de Basque was originally adapted to Polka-Mazurka music.
The polka-mazurka is a historical dance form that is no longer practised as a living social tradition.

sections.origins_and_history: Wotagei originated in the 1970s and 1980s from shin'eitai cheering squads. The practice of MIX, a patterned call, was established around 1993. The 2002 song 'Romantic Ukare Mode' became the most associated track with the dance, leading to a viral performance outside the Saitama Super Arena in 2004.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers, known as uchishi, use glow sticks or penlights to create light trails. Techniques are divided into chorus-based moves like thundersnake, muramasa, and amaterasu, and non-chorus moves like OAD and PPPH. Movements involve jumping, clapping, and arm-waving.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is exclusively Japanese idol pop, including artists from Hello! Project, AKB48, and Vocaloid. The music is characterized by high energy, specific instrumental breaks for MIX, and vocal-heavy arrangements.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers often use glow sticks (cyalume) or penlights. Performances occur at concerts, anime conventions, and dedicated street spaces. Some fans wear specialized gear like decorated coats or headbands.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Wotagei is a form of fan support and artistic expression. It is performed to show dedication to idols, seiyuu (voice actresses), and during anime-related events.
sections.notable_figures: GinyuforcE (pioneers of cyalume dance), Kita no Uchishitachi, Fly-N, Zero-uchi Restart, and the individual known as 戰鬥哥 (Zhàndòu Gē).
sections.regional_variants: Not described in sources, though the practice has spread globally to Asia and North America.
sections.lineage: Developed from ōendan (sporting cheering squads) and shin'eitai (idol cheering groups).

teaching.level_notes: Beginners should start with basic chorus techniques like romance and thundersnake.

claims.text: Wotagei (ヲタ芸), also known as otagei (オタ芸), is a type of dancing and cheering gestures performed by wota, fans of Japanese idol singers.
Wotagei is particularly associated with fans of Hello! Project, AKB48, and Vocaloid idols including Hatsune Miku.
Wotagei itself originated with shin'eitai cheering groups for idols around the 1970s and 1980s, whose members shouted calls in unison.
The practice of MIX, the specific pattern of calls during intros and instrumental breaks, started at idol venues around 1993.
GinyuforcE, originally formed in 2009 as Ginyu Tokusentai (ギニュ～特戦隊), were described as pioneers of cyalume dance.
In October 2019, Cyalume Dance received a Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Award in the arts and education field.

sections.origins_and_history: The era began in the early 19th century, influenced by Romanticism in Europe. It is traditionally dated from 1815 to 1870, with the 1832 premiere of La Sylphide in Paris serving as a primary catalyst.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers utilized early pointe work to create an ethereal, floating effect. The movement style is characterized by soft, rounded arms, a forward tilt of the upper body, and elaborate leg movements.
sections.music_and_instruments: Early ballets often used pastiche music, but the era evolved to include specially written scores. Adolphe Adam introduced the leitmotif, and composers like Léo Delibes later contributed to the genre's musical sophistication.
sections.costume_and_setting: The Romantic tutu, a long, white, multi-layered tulle skirt, is the signature costume. Settings often featured supernatural, moonlit landscapes, enhanced by the introduction of gas lighting.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The ballets focused on the dichotomy between the real world and the spiritual realm. Plots frequently involved spirit women who enslaved the hearts of mortal men.
sections.notable_figures: Marie Taglioni, Carlotta Grisi, Lucille Grahn, Fanny Cerrito, Pauline Leroux, Fanny Elssler, and choreographers like Jules Perrot and Filippo Taglioni.
sections.regional_variants: While centered in Paris and London, the style spread across Europe. Denmark maintained a tradition where male dancers remained more prominent than in the French scene.
sections.lineage: Succeeded the 'ballet d'action' of the 18th century and preceded the 'grand ballet' of the late 19th century.

claims.text: The Romantic ballet is defined primarily by an era in ballet in which the ideas of Romanticism in art and literature influenced the creation of ballets.
It is typically considered to have begun with the 1832 début in Paris of the ballerina Marie Taglioni in the ballet La Sylphide.
The Romantic era marked the rise of the ballerina as a central part of ballet, where previously men had dominated performances.
The costume for the Romantic ballerina was the romantic tutu, a full, white, multi-layered skirt made of tulle.
The Romantic ballet abandoned Greek myths in favor of Norse mythology.
Adolphe Adam was a pioneer in using the leitmotif in ballet.
Arthur Saint-Léon's 1870 ballet Coppélia is considered to be the last work of the Romantic Ballet.

sections.origins_and_history: The genre originated in the 19th century in Lima, specifically within the Malambo district of the Rimac district. It developed through the fusion of European waltz styles with Afro-Peruvian and indigenous musical elements during the 'Guardia Vieja' period (1900-1920).

sections.occasions_and_meaning: The music serves as a symbol of Peruvian culture, with lyrics reflecting the cultural personality, conflicts, and values of the urban working class.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Felipe Pinglo Alva, Chabuca Granda, Augusto Polo Campos, Eva Ayllón, and Arturo 'Zambo' Cavero.
sections.regional_variants: The genre spread to Chile, where it influenced 'música cebola', and to Argentina, where it influenced the local tango community.
sections.lineage: Derived from the European waltz, influenced by Afro-Peruvian rhythms, and later incorporating elements of blues, fox-trot, and tango.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated from the Romani people of Granada and Almería, evolving from earlier Morisco dance styles. It was suppressed during the 16th-century Inquisition but continued to be practiced in secret.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform barefoot, utilizing finger cymbals. The movement is characterized by a slow, heavy rhythm with similarities to belly dancing, focusing on the fluidity of the skirt.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is typically a slow, binary-meter flamenco style, often described as a slow tango. Key instruments include the guitar and sonajas (finger cymbals).
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear a blouse tied under the bust and a long skirt fitted at the hips with wide pleats. It is traditionally performed in the caves of Sacromonte.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically, the Zambra was a staple of Romani wedding ceremonies. It is now frequently performed as a cultural attraction in the caves of Granada.
sections.notable_figures: Carmen Amaya, Lola Flores, Manolo Caracol, La Chunga, and Pilar López Júlvez are recognized for adopting and popularizing the style.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is primarily associated with the Sacromonte district in Granada and the cave dwellings of Almería.
sections.lineage: The dance is considered a descendant of Morisco dance traditions, later assimilated by Romani groups.

claims.text: Zambra is a style of flamenco dance, typical of the Romani people of the provinces of Granada and Almería.
It is believed that the zambra is a continuation of earlier Morisco styles of dance.
The dance was prohibited in Spain in the 16th century during the Inquisition for political reasons.
The dance is performed barefoot with finger cymbals, a blouse tied under the bust, and a long skirt.
In modern times, it has been espoused by flamenco dancers Carmen Amaya and Lola Flores.
The Zambra was a national dance, to which the Moors were enthusiastically attached.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated from Iban ancestors observing the common hill myna and the great argus, leading to the creation of 'Bungai Ajat' and 'Bunga Ajat' movements. It is believed to be associated with the Iban ethnic group since the 16th century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is characterized by graceful, bird-like movements. Male dancers perform with shields and swords, often swinging their bodies. Female dancers use the Pua Kumbu fabric as a central display. Specific movements include jumping in circles and, in the case of Ngajat Lesong, lifting a heavy wooden mortar with the teeth.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical ensemble includes large and medium gongs (tawak and bebendai), drums (ketebung/dumba), a set of small gongs (engkromong), and the belikan string instrument.
sections.costume_and_setting: Male dancers wear 'gagung' (thick vests of animal skin) and feathered headdresses. Female dancers wear 'ngepan' headdresses, chest hooks, and bracelets. Performances often take place on the 'tanju' (outer platform) of a longhouse or on a stage.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ngajat is performed for Gawai harvest festivals, to welcome guests, and historically to celebrate the return of warriors. It serves as a manifestation of masculinity, strength, and community identity.
sections.notable_figures: Dion Das Louis, an eight-year-old dancer from Sarawak who won two gold medals at the 2024 World Performing Arts Championships.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include Ngajat Serakup (standardized stage version), Ngajat Bebunoh (warrior/hunting replication), Ngajat Lesong (strength display), Ngajat Induk (female-led ritual), and Ngajat Ngalu Temuai (welcome dance).
sections.lineage: The dance is a traditional Iban practice, with modern stage versions like Ngajat Serakup developed by the Dayak Dance and Cultural Association.

claims.text: The Ngajat is a traditional dance performed by the Iban community of Sarawak in Malaysia.
The ancestors of the Iban community dreamed of coming to a remote village and followed the movements of the common hill myna and the great argus to create the dance.
The dance is strongly believed to be associated with the Iban ethnic group since the 16th century.
Male dancers often wear elaborate headdresses with feathers, shields such as terabai, and a variety of swords.
Ngajat Lesong illustrates the manifestation of power and masculinity in Iban males by lifting a wooden rice mortar with their teeth.
Ngajat is a living tradition, with practitioners winning international awards in the 21st century.

sections.origins_and_history: The Vannam originated as recitations ('varnana') and were later adapted into solo dances. Their development was significantly encouraged by King Sri Weeraparakrama Narendrasinghe (1707-1739). The lyrics for the eighteen principal Vannam were composed by the sage Ganithalankara.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Vannam are performed as solo dances. The dancer uses movements and gestures to describe the behavior of the subject, such as animals or deities, while the accompanying song provides the narrative background.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features the Geta Bera (a tapered, hand-played drum) and Thalampataa (cymbals). The rhythm is central, and the dancer performs to the song's lyrics.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances traditionally took place in a 'kavikara maduwa', a decorated dance arena. The full 'ves' costume is only awarded to dancers who have mastered all eighteen Vannam.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Vannam are inspired by nature, history, legend, folk religion, and sacred lore. Each dance aims to express a specific 'rasaya' (sentiment or mood).
sections.notable_figures: King Sri Weeraparakrama Narendrasinghe and the sage Ganithalankara are the primary figures associated with the formalization of the eighteen Vannam.
sections.regional_variants: There are eighteen classical Vannam, with later additions including the Samanala (butterfly), Mahabo (sacred bo tree), and Hansa (swan) Vannam.
sections.lineage: Vannam belongs to the Kandyan dance (Uda Rata Natum) tradition of Sri Lanka.

claims.text: There are 18 vannam in the Kandyan dance form.
Originally a vannam was a kind of recitation.
The word vannam comes from the Sinhala word varnana ('descriptive praise').
Traditionally a dancer would have to learn to perform all of these vannam before they would be gifted the ves costume.
It is said that the kavi (poetry sung to music) for the eighteen principal vannam were composed by an old sage named Ganithalankara.
History reveals that the Kandyan king Sri Weeraparakrama Narendrasinghe gave considerable encouragement to dance and music.

sections.origins_and_history: The Sneak-Up Dance is a traditional dance performed within the context of the Pow Wow, a gathering of dancers and singers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance follows a pattern of drum rolls and Omaha beats. During drum rolls, dancers shake bells and perform gestures of seeking an enemy. During Omaha beats, dancers advance toward the center, stopping on the final beat of the song, then returning to the perimeter.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided by the drum and singers, utilizing specific drum rolls and the standard Omaha beat.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear regalia including bells and roach crest feathers, which must be kept spinning through head movements.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed at Pow Wows as a demonstration of skill and traditional narrative, often in a competitive context.

claims.text: The Sneak-Up Dance follows a definite pattern of drum rolls in the first half of the four renditions and a standard Omaha beat in the second half of each of the four renditions.
On the drum roll, the dancers shake their bells and make gestures of either following or seeking out the enemy.
On the Omaha beats, they sneak up, advancing toward the center and stopping on the last beat of the song, then walking back to the perimeter.
The fourth rendition doesn’t end as the first three do, but continues with three or four straight Omaha renditions.
The purpose of this action is to keep the roach crest feathers spinning. To keep the feathers moving constantly is the sign of a good dancer.
Although the Omaha is a freestyle type of dancing, dancers must follow the changing beat of the drum and stop when the music does, with both feet on the ground.

sections.origins_and_history: Locking began in the late 1960s in Los Angeles when Don Campbell combined fad dances with his own accidental 'lock' freezes. The group The Lockers, featuring members like Toni Basil and Fred 'Mr. Penguin' Berry, propelled the style to national fame via television. By the 1990s, the dance was revitalized in Europe and Japan, moving from club floors to international competition stages.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Locking is performed solo or in groups, emphasizing a 'lock'—a brief, sharp freeze following a fast movement. Dancers use a mix of loose, rhythmic hip and leg movements with tight, controlled arm and wrist actions. Key stylistic elements include pointing, wrist twirls, and comical facial expressions. Beginners start by mastering the basic 'lock' position and the 'point' gesture.
sections.music_and_instruments: Locking is danced to traditional funk music, specifically tracks produced or performed by artists like James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone. The music is characterized by a strong, rhythmic beat that allows for the sharp, syncopated freezes central to the dance.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditional attire includes loud striped socks, pegged pants, bright colorful satin shirts with large collars, big bow ties, and white gloves. Large 'Apple Boy' hats or berets are also iconic. The dance originated in nightclubs like Maverick's Flat.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Locking is a performance-oriented social dance. It is meant to be entertaining, with dancers often engaging the audience through humor, mime, and direct interaction. It is a staple of funk-style competitions like Juste Debout and Summer Dance Forever.
sections.notable_figures: Don Campbell (founder), The Lockers (foundational group), Jimmy 'Scoo B Doo' Foster, Alpha Anderson, Anthony 'Skeeter Rabbit' Higgins, and Toni Basil.
sections.regional_variants: While the core style remains consistent, regional variations developed in London, New York City, and Japan, where local crews like the Shack Crew and Magnificent Force added unique stylistic signatures.
sections.lineage: Locking is a funk-style dance that draws inspiration from 1960s social dances like the Funky Chicken, the Jerk, and the Mashed Potato.

basic_steps: The Lock: Bending slightly forward with arms forming a circle downward.

teaching.rhythm: Lockers often put a small pause and move up on the second and fourth beats to emphasize the locking.

teaching.level_notes: Requires high physical fitness and knee protection for floor work.

sections.origins_and_history: The Nago tradition stems from the Yoruba people brought to Haiti during the Atlantic slave trade. The term 'Nago' is derived from 'Anagó', a historic exonym for the Yoruba. The tradition represents a syncretization of Yoruba orisha and rites into the Haitian Vodou framework.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features strong thrusting, swaying, shoulder undulations, and pirouettes combined with fast footwork. It is performed to the rhythm of three Rada cowhide-head drums.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is provided by three Rada cowhide-head drums. Rhythmic patterns include the fast-paced Nago Chaud and the slow, heavy Nago Grand Coup.
sections.costume_and_setting: Nago rites necessitate an iron zin, a ceremonial cooking pot, instead of the typical clay vessel used in other Vodou rituals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Nago rituals are marked by the call 'Awo che Nago'. The dance honors the militant, masculine Ogou spirits, who are associated with the elements of earth, fire, and metal.
sections.notable_figures: Loco, known as the 'king of the Nago' (wa Nago), is the leader of the Nago nanchon. The Ogou are the dominant group of lwa within the nanchon.
sections.regional_variants: Veneration of the Nago as a wholly distinct nation is more typical of Northern Haitian Vodou, whereas in other areas, it is often absorbed into Rada or Petwo rites.
sections.lineage: The tradition is a syncretization of Yoruba religion, specifically the orisha, into the Haitian Vodou nanchon system.

For Haitian Vodou drumming in the Nago rite, three Rada cowhide-head drums are needed.
Nago rites necessitate an iron zin instead of the typical clay vessel.
The leader of the Nago nanchon is the lwa Loco, called the 'king of the Nago' (wa Nago).

sections.origins_and_history: Yanvalou originates from the Fon and Mahi peoples of present-day Benin, West Africa, and was brought to Haiti as part of the Vodou tradition.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is characterized by a low center of gravity with bent knees. The primary movement is a spinal undulation that flows from the head to the pelvis, often with hands placed on the knees.
sections.music_and_instruments: The rhythm is played on a set of three percussion instruments: the maman, the seconde (or segun), and the boula (or bass) drums, accompanied by an ogan (iron bell).
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Yanvalou is performed during Rada rituals to honor the lwa Damballah (serpent spirit of fertility) and Agwé (deity of the sea).
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: Variations include Yanvalou Fran (base), Yanvalou debout (standing), Yanvalou des bas (squatting), Yanvalou z'epaules (shoulder dance), Yanvalou Gede (for the Festival of the Dead), and Yanvalou Maskowan (advanced).
sections.lineage: Derived from the Fon and Mahi peoples of Benin.

sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in troupes with rows of male and female couples. Dancers perform a variety of steps to the beat of a band. It is a courtship ritual.

sections.costume_and_setting: Female dancers wear garments finely embroidered with colorful natural motifs and distinctive hats. Male dancers wear overlapping women’s skirts, military shirts, slings, and 'strong hats'.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed during religious festivities throughout the rainy season. It coincides with the beginning of the agricultural production cycle and symbolizes the renewal of nature and society.

claims.text: The Wititi dance of the Colca Valley is a traditional folk dance associated with the beginning of adult life.
It takes the form of a courtship ritual and is typically performed by young people during religious festivities celebrated throughout the rainy season.
It is danced in troupes with rows of male and female couples performing a variety of steps to the beat of a band.
Female dancers wear garments finely embroidered with colourful natural motifs and distinctive hats, while male dancers wear overlapping women’s skirts, military shirts, slings and ‘strong hats’.
The dance coincides with the beginning of the agricultural production cycle and symbolizes the renewal of nature and society.
The Wititi dance of the Colca Valley is learned through direct observation by youth and children in school and at private family gatherings, such as christenings, birthdays and weddings.

sections.origins_and_history: The 'upa'upa originated in Tahiti, where the term broadly designated dance in Tahitian dictionaries. Early accounts closely link it to the Arioi, a wandering brotherhood devoted to the sacred pig deities Orotetefa and Urutetefa who traveled between islands staging pantomimes, songs, and dances. Following the 1797 arrival of London Missionary Society missionaries, the dance was condemned, and the Pōmare Code of 1819 formally banned it as immoral. Queen Pōmare IV's Tahitian Code of 1842 renewed the absolute prohibition, ordering that houses used for dancing be converted into public halls for prayer, schooling, or judicial assemblies. French colonial ordinances in 1849, 1853, and 1876 maintained bans or restricted performances under strict permits issued only to chiefs for Saturday nights. Despite suppression, clandestine dancing persisted throughout the nineteenth century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances typically feature groups of paired boys and girls executing movements described in historical accounts as sexually oriented or passionate mime. The dance was traditionally directed by a leader or game master. It begins on a slow, measured cadence accompanied by distinct gestures, gradually accelerating and amplifying in volume and tempo toward a state of high excitement. Dancers perform barefoot, executing rapid, whirling movements concentrated in the thighs, knees, and lower back (reins), accompanied by full-body shaking, articulated posturing, and vocal cries.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for the 'upa'upa relies primarily on human voice, flutes, and drums (tam-tam). Accounts describe the instrumental accompaniment as a driving, rhythmic accompaniment of flute and drum, which supported vocal chants led by a performance master over many continuous hours.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historic Arioi presentations were recorded as occurring with naked performers and onlookers. In 1872, Pierre Loti recorded dancers performing barefoot in royal palace gardens wearing festive gowns and flower crowns. By 1900, dancers incorporated traditional materials into garments resembling ponchos or mother Hubbard dresses. Around 1920, raffia strips were integrated, evolving into the characteristic skirt known as the moré, made from hibiscus fibers. Male dancers were subsequently permitted bare torsos.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance was performed during Arioi touring spectacles, public celebrations, and major social rites such as weddings, where festivities commenced on the eve of the nuptials and extended across multiple days and nights. Beyond theatrical entertainment representing mythological and romantic narratives, the dance functioned as a communal expression of joy and celebration.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical figures include Queen Pōmare IV, who enacted legal bans in 1842; missionary William Ellis, who documented Arioi spectacles in 1829; writer Pierre Loti, who witnessed garden performances in 1872; Antoine Mathivet (Monchoisy), who published detailed movement descriptions in 1888; and Madeleine Mou'a, who founded the troupe Heiva in 1956 under the patronage of Princesses Teri'i and Takau.
sections.regional_variants: The dance flourished in Tahiti and extended across the Society Islands, including the Leeward Islands, which mirrored Tahiti's legal restrictions. In 1912, filmmaker Gaston Méliès recorded a variant performance on Rarotonga in the Cook Islands.
sections.lineage: The 'upa'upa is the historical predecessor of the modern Tahitian tāmūrē and directly informed the repertoire revived by Madeleine Mou'a in the mid-twentieth century.

sections.origins_and_history: Wolosso arose in 2006 in Ivory Coast as a popular dance style that rapidly spread throughout West Africa. Historically, the style represents a synthesis of traditional African folk dances and Western pop dance culture.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed through isolated circular hip movements. Female dancers periodically lower the upper body, placing heavy emphasis on the buttocks. The movement operates over an offbeat-accented 4/4 meter, at moderate to fast musical pacing between 40 and 70 bpm.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance relies on an offbeat-emphasized 4/4 rhythm that is often layered with polyrhythmic counters typical of African folk traditions. The musical tempo is positioned between 40 and 70 bpm. Various Wolosso musicians have faced criticism for incorporating sexually explicit lyrical content.
sections.costume_and_setting: Wolosso belongs to contemporary urban popular culture and secular social dancing. Over time, the term broadened to designate revealing, permissive styles of dress and unconventional lifestyles, especially among women.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance functions as a contemporary social dance. In predominantly Muslim countries of West Africa, Wolosso has stirred strong public offense due to movements perceived as lascivious. Stripped of their original ritual and folk contexts, these bodily articulations are frequently identified with decadent Western culture.

sections.origins_and_history: Zydeco originated in the beginning of the 20th century among the Francophone Creole peoples of south central and southwest Louisiana as a folk dance style linked to heavily syncopated zydeco music.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Zydeco is danced as a partner dance where the follower usually mirrors the leader's steps, though figures allow for self-expression and improvisation. Dancers execute small sidewise steps with a relatively steady upper body, keeping the physical feel directed downward into the floor without hip wiggling, swinging, or jumping. The eight-beat basic cycle is organized as two mirrored four-beat sections ('SPSS SPSS', meaning step-pause-step-step, or slow-quick-quick). Count 1-2 shifts weight slowly to the lead's left foot, beat 3 moves quickly to the right, and beat 4 shifts quickly to the left, repeating on the opposite foot on beats 5-8. Dancers rotate clockwise or shuffle in place, filling the pauses on beats 2 and 6 with knee bends, hip drops, or 'eat-a-beat' foot variations like heel taps, kicks, brushes, and twists.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance corresponds directly to heavily syncopated zydeco music, which accents the second and sixth beats within an eight-count rhythm. Specific musical instruments are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: It is primarily danced socially in community spaces and sometimes in stage performances. Specific costumes are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance serves as a social gathering practice and an avenue for personal improvisation and self-expression within Creole culture.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: The dance emerged across south central and southwest Louisiana, but specific regional stylistic variants are not described in sources.
sections.lineage: Zydeco evolved from Creole folk dance roots into a distinctive partner dance characterized by a downward feel opposite to swing or ballroom styles.

sections.origins_and_history: Waacking originated in Los Angeles during the early 1970s inside LGBTQ+ nightclubs, created primarily by African American and Latino dancers. It began as punking, a name derived from a derogatory slur aimed at gay men, which performers inverted into an expressive, narrative dance style. Dancers moved to underground and imported disco music that DJs sped up to produce an intense, energetic atmosphere. The specific technique of driving the arms over the head in rhythm became known as 'whack'. Heterosexual dancers who encountered the style renamed it whacking to distance themselves from anti-gay terminology, after which gay culture reclaimed and reshaped the term into 'waacking', formalized when Soul Train dancer and singer-songwriter Jeffrey Daniel added the 'g'. During the 1980s and 1990s, the AIDS crisis killed most of the style's iconic pioneers, driving the dance close to extinction until Brian 'Footwork' Green began teaching it in 2003 to ensure its transmission.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The style is executed through rapid, rotational arm sweeps, explosive rhythmic strikes, and theatrical poses coordinated with music. Dancers whip their forearms and wrists around and behind the head and across the shoulder line, isolating sharp gestures while maintaining rhythmic syncopation. A key technical element is posing, in which dancers freeze into glamorous, heightened diva stances inspired by Hollywood movie figures. The dance prioritizes facial expression, sensuality, and dramatic storytelling, allowing the performer to embody distinct attitudes and narrative moods. Footwork in the sources incorporates elements derived from jazz, gymnastics, martial arts, and hip-hop influences, though the central visual hallmark remains overhead arm isolations danced to fast tempos.
sections.music_and_instruments: Waacking was founded on 1970s disco and funk, specifically underground and imported disco records that were often sped up on club turntables to increase dance floor energy. Over subsequent decades, the dance adapted to 1980s post-disco, electro sounds, and modern music varieties, though disco remains its historical and primary sonic foundation. The music is characterized by steady four-on-the-floor percussion, driving basslines, orchestral sweeps, and brass hits that provide sharp rhythmic accents for explosive arm strikes and sudden poses.
sections.costume_and_setting: Originally performed in dimly lit LGBTQ+ nightclubs of 1970s Los Angeles, waacking was framed by social freedom and theatrical display. Dancers drew visual and sartorial inspiration from classic Hollywood screen stars such as Marlene Dietrich, Lauren Bacall, and James Dean, adopting vintage diva attitudes, tailored silhouettes, and stylized garments. In modern practice, waacking appears in international dance battles, television studios, university theatre departments, music videos, and competitive ice rinks, where performers continue to wear expressive, high-fashion, and dramatic attire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: In its original gay club context, punking and waacking served as an outlet of creative liberation, sensual expression, and self-definition for marginalized queer, Black, and Latino dancers facing social hostility. The dance provided a theatrical space to emulate glamorous Hollywood divas and enact personal stories through heightened physicality. Today, waacking is performed at competitive street dance battles, theatre showcases, university dance curricula, pop concerts, and global sports ceremonies, retaining its ethos of unapologetic self-expression and dramatic presence.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical and contemporary figures include Jeffrey Daniel, who added the 'g' to the name; Tyrone Proctor (1953–2020), a pioneering Los Angeles creator and Soul Train dancer; Brian 'Footwork' Green, who initiated the 2003 global revival through workshops; Kumari Suraj, who choreographed a milestone 2011 routine on So You Think You Can Dance; and French waacker Josépha Madoki, who danced in the 2018 'Apeshit' music video by Beyoncé and Jay-Z. Other notable practitioners named in sources include Bruno Marignan, Sandrine Sainte Croix, Lil Kiss, Princess Lockeroo, Mariana Benenge, Mounia Nassangar, Habibitch, Boubou, choreographer Axelle Munezero, and Olympic champions Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron.
sections.regional_variants: Waacking originated in Los Angeles, California, developing alongside New York City's parallel ballroom voguing culture on the East Coast of the United States. While early waacking was centered in southern California venues and national broadcast sets like Soul Train, contemporary regional hubs have expanded globally. France has emerged as a significant center through artists like Josépha Madoki, Princess Lockeroo, and choreographers who adapted the style for theater and international competition.
sections.lineage: Waacking evolved directly out of punking in 1970s Los Angeles gay clubs, absorbing stylistic and physical principles from jazz dance, gymnastics, martial arts, and Hollywood screen performance. It developed alongside locking within the Los Angeles street dance ecosystem and runs historically parallel to East Coast voguing. In modern lineages, waacking has exchanged vocabulary with hip-hop dance and entered university dance departments as well as commercial performance repertoires.

claims.text: Waacking originated from punking, a dance created in the gay clubs of Los Angeles during the 1970s disco era.
The movement was characterized by moving the arms rhythmically over the head.
Jeffrey Daniel modified the name from waackin to waacking.
Dancers took stylistic inspiration from classic Hollywood screen stars.
The dance style was developed by the LGBTQ+ community, especially African American and Latino dancers.
The AIDS crisis in the 1980s and 1990s killed most iconic dancers, leading waacking to almost disappear.
Brian Green began teaching waacking in 2003 to address the lack of transmission.
Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron won gold at the 2022 Winter Olympics with a program influenced by waacking.

sections.origins_and_history: Ballet de cour developed in late 16th-century France out of medieval processions, mummeries, and Italian Renaissance court festivals. Catherine de' Medici championed these entertainments following her 1533 marriage to Henri II, bringing Italian staging concepts to Paris. The Académie de Poésie et de Musique, established in 1570 by Jean-Antoine de Baif and Thibault de Courville, provided the philosophical ambition to harmonize dance, verse, and music. Key early spectacles included the Ballet des Polonais in 1573 and the Ballet Comique de la Reine in 1581, directed by Balthasar de Beaujoyeulx. Production expanded under Louis XIII and reached its political apex under Louis XIV and Cardinal Mazarin, with Isaac de Benserade authoring texts. The genre faded after Louis XIV withdrew from dancing in 1670.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances occurred in great halls with the audience stacked on three surrounding tiers, making overhead geometric floor designs central to the choreography. Dancers executed intricate patterns, swerves, sinuosities, interlacings, confrontations, and retreats. The work unfolded in structured entrées where performers danced by turn, culminating in the Grand Ballet with the entire cast, followed by an open social ball where spectators joined the performers. Specific individual foot mechanics, counts, and step names for the earliest period are not described in sources beyond Beaujoyeulx's use of measure and geometry, Thoinot Arbeau's 1589 foundations, and Pierre Beauchamp's subsequent codification of the five positions.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical framework encompassed vocal and instrumental pieces, featuring an opening overture with recitation followed by vocal airs, choruses, and instrumental dances accompanying each entrée. Violins and court instrumental ensembles accompanied the dancers. Central composers across the era included Pierre Guédron, Antoine Boësset, Étienne Moulinié, Michael Praetorius, and Jean-Baptiste Lully, whose collaborations with Pierre Beauchamp elevated ballet music to an equal partner with movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Spectacles were staged in large palace halls, such as the Tuileries Palace and the Louvre, before the advent of the proscenium stage. Decor was lavish, featuring elaborate scenic machinery such as chariot-floats, palaces, gardens, townscapes, and three-tiered fountains. Costumes were ornate aristocratic dress, later evolving toward lighter apparel and flexible footwear by the late 17th century.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ballets de cour marked royal weddings, state receptions of foreign ambassadors, and celebrations of political triumphs. As a secular ceremony designed to exalt the State and project royal power, it communicated harmony, virtue, and monarchical dominance, often using classical allegory to symbolize national reconciliation after religious civil strife.
sections.notable_figures: Key historic figures include Queen Catherine de' Medici; choreographer and master of revels Balthasar de Beaujoyeulx (Baldassarino de Belgioioso); poet Isaac de Benserade; Académie founders Jean-Antoine de Baif and Thibault de Courville; monarchs Henri III, Louis XIII, and Louis XIV; composer Jean-Baptiste Lully; and ballet superintendent Pierre Beauchamp.
sections.regional_variants: Originating in the French royal court in Paris and its royal residences (such as the Tuileries, the Louvre, and Chantilly), the form rapidly spread to courts across Europe, contrasting with Italian opera which concentrated more heavily on singing than physical choreography.
sections.lineage: Evolved from medieval mummeries and Italian Renaissance court festivals into French court ballet; later transformed into comédie-ballet and opéra-ballet, directly providing the technical and organizational foundation for codified classical ballet.

claims.text: Ballet de cour is the term given to ballets performed at royal courts during the 16th and 17th centuries.
The early ballet de cour was a secular event whose primary political objective was the exaltation of the state.
Early choreographies were designed as geometric figures meant to be observed from above by audiences seated on three sides.
In 1573, Catherine de' Medici commissioned the Ballet des Polonais, performed by sixteen noblewomen representing the sixteen provinces of France.
The five-hour Ballet Comique de la Reine was staged in 1581 to celebrate the wedding of Marguerite of Lorraine and the Duc de Joyeuse.
The 17th-century court ballet was structured with an overture, thematic entrées, and a final Grand Ballet.
When Louis XIV stopped dancing in court productions in 1670, it dealt a fatal blow to ballet de cour and gave rise to comédie-ballet and opéra-ballet.

sections.origins_and_history: The farruca developed as a flamenco style in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The word relates to 'farruco', an Andalusian term applied to immigrants from Galicia or Asturias, as well as a familiar nickname for Francisco. While lyric references to Galician bagpipes and landscape led many to claim a northern origin, musicologists note this has not been scientifically proven. Instead, it was adapted into flamenco (aflamencado) within theatrical venues, zarzuela, and cafés cantantes like Café Madrid and Café del Recreo in Cádiz. In 1907, composer José Serrano included a farruca in his sainete Alma de Dios. In 1908, dancer Faíco and guitarist Ramón Montoya consolidated the canonical dance and guitar forms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The farruca is danced as a dramatic solo characterized by upright posture, sharp footwork (zapateado), held poses, sudden pauses, turns, and abrupt directional changes. Performed within an eight-beat compás consisting of two 4/4 bars with accents on 1, 3, 5, and 7, it begins at a moderate, articulated tempo. Choreographies proceed from an entrance (salida) into marked compás, llamadas, remates, and extended escobillas. Dancers use double-time footwork, contratiempos, and level changes, driving through an acceleration (subida) toward a final llamada or cierre, sometimes finishing with the rhythm of a tanguillo or rumba.
sections.music_and_instruments: Farruca music is grounded in binary or quadruple meter (two measures of 4/4) with strong accents on counts 1, 3, 5, and 7. The primary accompanying instrument is the flamenco guitar, traditionally played in A minor or E minor, characterized by alternation between E7 and A minor, rasgueados, falsetas, and golpes. While often performed as an instrumental piece without cante, traditional verses feature four octosyllabic lines with assonant rhyme, descending contours on final vowels, and vocables such as 'tran tran tran treiro'.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance emerged within theatrical spaces, varieté, and cafés cantantes before transitioning to concert halls and ballet stages. Performers wear attire that accentuates vertical line and sharp posture, traditionally consisting of high-waisted trousers, fitted waistcoats, and flamenco boots suitable for virtuosic footwork. Historical descriptions document the use of a cape during early male stage performances. Early female dancers frequently performed the dance dressed in male clothing.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Farruca carries an austere, dramatic, and sombre character linked symbolically to valor and restraint. Unlike communal festive palos, it is primarily a theatrical and concert performance form. Its dramatic gravity was spotlighted in major theatrical works, including Manuel de Falla's 1919 ballet El sombrero de tres picos (as the Miller's Dance / Danse du meunier) choreographed by Léonide Massine, and Carlos Saura's film Carmen featuring Antonio Gades.
sections.notable_figures: Dancer Faíco (Francisco Mendoza Ríos) and guitarist Ramón Montoya are recognized as the primary architects of the modern dance and guitar structure. Dancers El Gato, Antonio de Bilbao, Manolito la Rosa, El Batato, Antonio Gades, El Güito, Mario Maya, and Manolete further codified its stage aesthetic. Groundbreaking women dancers who reshaped the form include Rafaela Valverde 'La Tanguera', Carmen Amaya, and Sara Baras. Prominent guitar interpreters include Sabicas, Carlos Montoya, Paco Peña, Manolo Sanlúcar, and Paco de Lucía.
sections.regional_variants: Technique not described in sources beyond local café cantante traditions and theatrical adaptations.
sections.lineage: Farruca belongs to the aflamencado group of non-Andalusian folkloric forms along with the garrotín. It shares a binary 4/4 compás with tangos and tientos, the tempo feel of tanguillos, and occasionally adopts elements of rumba or tanguillo during its closing stretta.

basic_steps: Marcaje: Stand upright with severe posture, stepping through a controlled four-count pulse marking counts 1, 3, 5, and 7.
Llamada: Strike a sharp heel-toe combination ending with an abrupt stop to signal musical changes to the guitarist.
Zapateado Escobilla: Execute heel-and-toe strikes utilizing contratiempos and double-time subdivisions against the slow 8-count pulse.
Giro y Remate: Snap through a sharp spot turn and freeze into a low, held pose on the final closing beat.
teaching.rhythm: Binary/quadruple meter counted in two 4/4 bars across an 8-pulse cycle: [1] 2 [3] 4 [5] 6 [7] 8
teaching.formation: Solo
teaching.level_notes: Requires strong foot percussion technique, balance during abrupt halts, and strict compás retention at moderate to fast speeds.

claims.text: The farruca is a musical form of flamenco that developed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
The dancer Faíco and guitarist Ramón Montoya established the classic modern dance and guitar structure of the farruca.
The farruca compás is typically counted in two measures of 4/4 with primary accents on the odd counts.
Although historically associated with male bailaores, female dancers have expanded the form.
José Otero recorded the first description of the farruca in his 1912 dance treatise.
Faíco created the first choreography to music by Ramón Montoya in 1908.
Manuel de Falla featured the dance under the title Danse du meunier in his ballet El sombrero de tres picos.

episode_brief.title_hook: Silence, Strike, Defiance: The Farruca Solo
episode_brief.logline: Step inside the austere world of flamenco's most theatrical solo, born in early 1900s music halls from sharp heel strikes and absolute stillness.
beats: The opening guitar strikes an A minor chord in total stage darkness before a lone spotlight reveals a rigid, motionless silhouette.
Archival photographs show dancer Faíco and guitarist Ramón Montoya crafting the form in early twentieth-century Madrid and Seville.
The instructor breaks down the fundamental 8-count pulse, isolating the distinctive odd-beat accents on counts 1, 3, 5, and 7.
Demonstration of the escobilla, revealing how slow foot strikes double in velocity while the upper body remains stone-still.
Exploration of groundbreaking women like Carmen Amaya who adopted trousers to reclaim the dance's ferocious technical intensity.
The performance reaches a fever pitch: an accelerating subida snaps instantly into silence on a single dramatic remate.

sections.origins_and_history: Yove male mome, also known as Povela e Yova, originates from the traditional dance Jove from the Shopluk region of Bulgaria. In 1966, US folk dance instructor Dennis Boxell introduced its choreography outside of Bulgaria at an event in Stockton, California. Following this introduction, the dance became widely popular among international folk dancers across the globe.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed as a fast, complicated line dance arranged in a curved line or open circle. Dancers link together by holding their neighbours by the belt, or by the hands if belts are not worn. Structurally, one common version consists of seven patterns containing four bars each. Dancers follow an 18/16 meter divided into alternating sub-bars of 7/16 and 11/16, counted as 3-2-2 and 2-2-3-2-2, or slow-quick-quick, quick-quick-slow-quick-quick.
sections.music_and_instruments: Musical renditions of Yove male mome are played in an 18/16 compound meter (7+11/16), incorporating alternating sub-bars of common chetvorno (7/16) and kopanitsa (11/16) rhythms. The melody and accompaniment often feature the traditional Bulgarian gaida (bagpipe). The accompanying lyrics belong to the folk song Povela e Yova, telling the story of Yova leading two horses to water.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance takes place in social and recreational settings in a curved line or open circle. In traditional contexts, dancers wear belts, which are essential for the traditional grip where each dancer holds their neighbours by the belt; handholds are used when belts are absent.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally danced to communal folk songs in the Shopluk region, the dance is tied to the lyrical narrative of Yova watering horses—giving clear water to her beloved's horse and murky water to her brother's horse. Today, it is widely performed at folk dance clubs, workshops, and recreational Balkan dance gatherings worldwide.
sections.notable_figures: US folk dance instructor Dennis Boxell played a pivotal role in disseminating the dance by introducing its choreography outside Bulgaria in Stockton, California, in 1966. Folklorist Manol Todorov documented the song's lyrics in his 1976 work Balgarska narodna muzika, and Bulgarian singer Hristina Boteva is known for performing the song.
sections.regional_variants: The dance originates from the Shopluk region of Bulgaria under the traditional name Jove. Beyond regional village variants, it is known under variant names such as Jove male mome, Jove malaj mome, and Povela e Yova.
sections.lineage: Yove male mome derives directly from the regional Shopluk dance Jove. Its rhythmic structure embeds the metrics of both chetvorno (7/16) and kopanitsa (11/16), representing a hybrid compound form within the broader family of Bulgarian horo line dances.

basic_steps: Grasp neighbouring dancers firmly by the belt or link hands if belts are not available.
Stand in an open circle or curved line facing slightly along the line of direction.
Execute the 7/16 sub-bar with a slow step on count 1 (three pulses) followed by two quick steps on counts 2 and 3 (two pulses each).
Execute the 11/16 sub-bar with two quick steps on counts 1 and 2 (two pulses each), one slow step on count 3 (three pulses), and two quick steps on counts 4 and 5 (two pulses each).
Progress through the seven choreographic patterns of four bars each while maintaining the line curvature.
teaching.formation: Curved line or open circle with belt hold (or hand hold)
teaching.level_notes: Requires mastery of asymmetric Balkan time signatures and rapid foot coordination across seven distinct patterns.

sections.origins_and_history: Tribal Fusion emerged from the California belly dance lineage tracing back to Jamila Salimpour, who founded the troupe Bal Anat in the late 1960s to present theatrical Middle Eastern and North African styles at California Renaissance fairs. Jamila taught Masha Archer of the San Francisco Classic Dance Troupe, who in turn taught Carolena Nericcio, the founder of FatChanceBellyDance and pioneer of American Tribal Style (ATS). In the late 1990s, Jill Parker—a student of Nericcio—founded Ultra Gypsy, considered the first tribal fusion dance company, scaling down the traditional costume and choreographing to contemporary DJ-mixed tracks. Simultaneously, Heather Stants introduced minimalist aesthetics and modern dance concepts through Urban Tribal Dance Company in 1999, while Rachel Brice codified the name 'Tribal Fusion' during email correspondence with Nericcio and popularized the movement globally.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Unlike the strictly group-led, cue-based structured improvisation of FatChanceBellyDance, Tribal Fusion is predominantly choreographed and can be performed as a solo, duet, or group piece. Dancers maintain an upright lifted posture while executing hyper-articulated isolations, including popping contractions, belly rolls, serpentine arm paths, and hip locks. Dancers integrate technique derived from Suhaila Salimpour, hip hop popping, flamenco arm carriage, and Indian classical forms like Kathak and Odissi. Movement shifts rapidly between slow, fluid muscular sinuosity and explosive percussive accents.
sections.music_and_instruments: Tribal Fusion evolved alongside late-1990s and early-2000s electronica, trip-hop, and world fusion. Producers and DJs merged traditional Middle Eastern acoustic instruments—such as darbuka, riqq, and oud—with synthesized beats, deep bass lines, and breakbeats. Key figures shaping the sound include Cheb i Sabbah, Bassnectar, Amon Tobin, Squarepusher, Solace (Jeremiah Soto), Pete List, and Beats Antique, creating what became known as the electronica Oriental genre.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costuming varies between rich maximalism and sleek modern minimalism. The adorned aesthetic, popularized by Mardi Love and The Indigo, features layered skirts, Tulle bi telli fabrics, antique tribal jewelry, Afghan guls, Indian shisha mirrors, and Rajasthani cowrie shells braided into the hair with dyed yarn. Tattoos, body piercings, and dramatic stage makeup are common. Conversely, the urban tribal branch championed by Heather Stants adopts minimalist, contemporary dance-inspired attire. Settings range from traditional haflas and belly dance festivals to theatrical stages and music festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Tribal Fusion is primarily a theatrical and performance art form rather than a social or ritual dance. It is performed on concert stages, community haflas, circus-theatre showcases, and alternative music events. Moving away from the commercial cabaret nightclub format, it emphasizes artistic self-expression, bodily mastery, strength, and female stage presence uncoupled from exoticized male-gaze entertainment.
sections.notable_figures: Seminal figures include Jill Parker ('mama of Tribal Fusion'), Heather Stants (founder of Urban Tribal Dance Company), Rachel Brice (foremost soloist and co-founder of The Indigo), Mardi Love (costume innovator and core member of The Indigo), Zoe Jakes (co-founder of Beats Antique), Suhaila Salimpour (whose isolation technique heavily influenced the movement), Ariellah Aflalo (Dark Fusion pioneer), and producer Miles Copeland.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include Urban Tribal, developed in San Diego with modern dance and street aesthetics; Dark Fusion, initiated by Ariellah Aflalo blending gothic elements; Vaudeville or Tribal Vintage, drawing from pre-WWII jazz, swing, and burlesque eras; and Improvisational Tribal Style (ITS), developed by Amy Sigil as an alternate group-improvisation framework.
sections.lineage: Traced through a direct teacher-student chain: Jamila Salimpour taught Masha Archer; Archer taught Carolena Nericcio (creator of ATS); Nericcio taught Jill Parker; Parker inspired Heather Stants and Mardi Love; technique was further shaped by Suhaila Salimpour; Rachel Brice consolidated these lines to form Tribal Fusion.

basic_steps: Lift ribcage and drop shoulders into an aligned, grounded stance with soft knees.
Execute an upper-torso chest slide side-to-side without moving the hips.
Roll the abdomen sequentially in an undulating belly roll, pulling inward from top to bottom.
Perform a sharp pelvic tuck and release isolation (lock or pop) on a percussive beat count.
Extend arms outward, creating continuous serpentine shoulder-to-wrist arm waves while maintaining torso stillness.
teaching.rhythm: Downtempo electronic 4/4 or syncopated world-fusion percussion; movement layers slow continuous undulations over sharp rhythmic locks.
teaching.formation: Solo performance, duet, or choreographed ensemble lines; does not require the lead-and-follow chorus formation of ATS.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on muscular isolation of the ribcage, pelvic locks, and decoupling arm movements from torso shifts.

claims.text: Tribal Fusion was created by fusing American Tribal Style belly dance and American Cabaret belly dance.
Jill Parker's company Ultra Gypsy was the first Tribal Fusion dance company.
In 1999 Heather Stants founded Urban Tribal Dance Company in San Diego with a minimalist aesthetic.
Mardi Love popularized Rajasthani cowrie falls using hand-dyed yarn for Tribal Fusion hair adornments.
Tribal Fusion is choreographed and can be performed as a solo.
The lineage runs from Jamila Salimpour through Masha Archer, Carolena Nericcio, Jill Parker, Heather Stants, and Mardi Love to Rachel Brice.
Tribal Fusion is an actively developing dance style practised today.
